The former passage betrays its derivative character by the fact that עלּיז is a word that belongs exclusively to Isaiah; whilst the latter is not only a compendium of <reference osisRef="Isa.66.20">Isa 66:20</reference>, but also points back to <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Isa 18:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference>, in the expression לנהרי־כוּשׁ מעבר. In Jeremiah, the indication of dependence upon Isaiah comes out most strongly in the prophecy against Babylon in Jer 50-51; ; in fact, it is so strong, that Movers, Hitzig, and De Wette regard the anonymous author of chapters 40-66 as the interpolator of this prophecy. But it also contains echoes of Isaiah 13-14; 21, and 34, and is throughout a Mosaic or earlier prophecies. The passage in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.1-Jer.10.16">Jer 10:1-16</reference> concerning the nothingness of the gods of the nations, sounds also most strikingly like Isaiah's; compare more especially <reference osisRef="Isa.44.12-Isa.44.15">Isa 44:12-15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.7">Isa 41:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.7">Isa 46:7</reference>, though the attempt has also been made to render this intelligible by the interpolation hypothesis. It is not only in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8">Isa 40:6-8</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Isa 40:10</reference>, which are admitted to be Jeremiah’s, that we meet with the peculiar characteristics of Jeremiah; but even in passages that are rejected we find such expressions of his as יפּה, אותם for אתּם, נבער, תּעתּעים, פּקדּה, a penal visitation, such as we never meet with in Isaiah II. And the whole of the consolatory words in <reference osisRef="Jer.30.10-Jer.30.11">Jer 30:10-11</reference>, and again in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.27-Jer.46.28">Jer 46:27-28</reference>, which sound so much like the deutero-Isaiah, are set down as having been inserted in the book of Jeremiah by Isaiah II. But Caspari has shown that this is impossible, because the concluding words of the promise, “I will correct thee in measure, and will not leave thee altogether unpunished,” would have no meaning at all if uttered at the close of the captivity; and also, because such elements as are evidently Jeremiah’s, and in which it coincides with prophecies of Jeremiah that are acknowledged to be genuine, far outweigh those of the deutero-Isaiah. And yet in this passage, when Israel is addressed as “my servant,” we hear the tone of the deutero-Isaiah. Jeremiah fuses in this instance, as in many other passages, the tones of Isaiah with his own. There are also many other passages which coincide with passages of the second part of Isaiah, both in substance and expression, though not so conclusively as those already quoted, and in which we have to decide between regarding Jeremiah as an imitator, or Isaiah II as an interpolator. But if we compare <reference osisRef="Jer.6.15">Jer 6:15</reference> with <reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Isa 56:11</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Isa.48.6">Isa 48:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.33.3">Jer 33:3</reference>, where Jeremiah, according to his usual custom, gives a different turn to the original passages by a slight change in the letters, we shall find involuntary reminiscences of Isaiah in Jeremiah, in such parallels as <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16">Jer 3:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.65.17">Isa 65:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.4.13">Jer 4:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.15">Isa 66:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jer 11:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Isa 53:1</reference>; and shall hear the ring of <reference osisRef="Isa.51.17-Isa.51.23">Isa 51:17-23</reference> in Jeremiah’s <hi type="italic">qı̄nōth</hi>, and that of Isaiah 56:9-57:11 <hi type="italic">a</hi> in the earlier reproachful addresses of Jeremiah, and not <hi type="italic">vice versa</hi>. <div eID="gen13313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13314" type="x-p"/> In conclusion, let us picture to ourselves the gradual development of Isaiah’s view of the <hi type="italic">captivity</hi>, that penal judgment already threatened in the law. (1.) In the <hi type="italic">Uzziah-Jotham</hi> age the prophet refers to the captivity, in the most general terms that can be conceived, in <reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">Isa 6:12</reference>, though he mentions it casually by its own name even in Isa 5:13. (2.) In the time of <hi type="italic">Ahaz</hi> we already see him far advanced beyond this first sketchy reference to the captivity. In Isa 11:11. he predicts a second deliverance, resembling the Egyptian Exodus. Asshur stands at the head of the countries of the <hi type="italic">diaspora</hi>, as the imperial power by which the judgment of captivity is carried out. (3.) In the early years of <hi type="italic">Hezekiah</hi>, <reference osisRef="Isa.22.18">Isa 22:18</reference> appears to indicate the carrying away of Judah by Asshur. But when the northern kingdom had succumbed to the judgment of the Assyrian banishment, and Judah had been mercifully spared this judgment, the eyes of Isaiah were directed to Babylon as the imperial power destined to execute the same judgment upon Judah. We may see this from <reference osisRef="Isa.39.5">Isa 39:5</reference>-7. Micah also speaks of Babylon as the future place of punishment and deliverance (Mic 4:10). The prophecies of the overthrow of Babylon in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.14">Isa 13:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.13.21">Isa 13:21</reference>, are therefore quite in the spirit of the prophecies of Hezekiah’s time. And chapters 40-66 merely develop on all sides what was already contained in germ in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.1-Isa.14.2">Isa 14:1-2</reference>; Isa 21:10. It is well known that in the time of Hezekiah Babylon attempted to break loose from Assyria; and so also the revolt of the Medes from Asshur, and the union of their villages and districts under one monarch named Deyoces, occurred in the time of Hezekiah.<note placement="foot">Spiegel (<hi type="italic">Eran</hi>, p. 313ff.) places the revolt of the Medes in the year 714, and Deyoces in the year 708.</note> <div eID="gen13314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13315" type="x-p"/> It is quite characteristic of Isaiah that he never names the Persians, who were at that time still subject to the Medes. He mentions <hi type="italic">Madai</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Isa 13:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">Isa 21:2</reference>, and <hi type="italic">Kōresh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Kurus</hi>), the founder of the Persian monarchy; but not that one of the two leading Iranian tribes, which gained its liberty through him in the time of Astyages, and afterwards rose to the possession of the imperial sway. <div eID="gen13315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13316" type="x-p"/> But how is it possible that Isaiah should have mentioned Cyrus by name centuries before this time (210 years, according to Josephus, <hi type="italic">Ant.</hi> xi. 1, 2)? Windischmann answers this question in his <hi type="italic">Zoroastrische Studien</hi>, p. 137. “No one,” he says, “who believes in a living, personal, omniscient God, and in the possibility of His revealing future events, will ever deny that He possesses the power to foretell the name of a future monarch.” And Albrecht Weber, the Indologian, finds in this answer “an evidence of self-hardening against the scientific conscience,” and pronounces such hardening nothing less than “devilish.” <div eID="gen13316" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13317" type="x-p"/> It is not possible to come to any understanding concerning this point, which is the real nerve of the prevailing settled conclusion as to chapters 40-66. We therefore hasten on to our exposition. <hi type="italic">And in relation to this, if we only allow that the prophet really was a prophet, it is of no essential consequence to what age he belonged</hi>. For in this one point we quite agree with the opponents of its genuineness, namely, that the standpoint of the prophet is the second half of the captivity. If the author is Isaiah, as we feel constrained to assume for reasons that we have already stated here and elsewhere, he is entirely carried away from his own times, and leads a pneumatic life among the exiles. There is, in fact, no more “Johannic” book in the whole of the Old Testament than this book of consolation. It is like the produce of an Old Testament gift of tongues. The fleshly body of speech has been changed into a glorified body; and we hear, as it were, spiritual voices from the world beyond, or world of glory. <div eID="gen13317" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">PART I. FIRST PROPHECY.— Chap 40. WORDS OF COMFORT, AND THE GOD OF COMPORT.</title> <div sID="gen13318" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference> In this first address the prophet vindicates his call to be the preacher of the comfort of the approaching deliverance, and explains this comfort on the ground that Jehovah, who called him to this comforting proclamation, was the incomparably exalted Creator and Ruler of the world. The first part of this address (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1-Isa.40.11">Isa 40:1-11</reference>) may be regarded as the prologue to the whole twenty-seven. The theme of the prophetic promise, and the irresistible certainty of its fulfilment, are here declared. Turning of the people of the captivity, whom Jehovah has neither forgotten nor rejected, the prophet commences thus in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference> : “<hi type="italic">Comfort ye, comfort ye may people, saith your God.</hi>” This is the divine command to the prophets. <hi type="italic">Nachămū</hi> (<hi type="italic">piel</hi>, literally, to cause to breathe again) is repeated, because of its urgency (<hi type="italic">anadiplosis</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.27">Isa 41:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.43.11">Isa 43:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.43.25">Isa 43:25</reference>, etc.). The word יאמר, which does not mean “will say” here (Hofmann, Stier), but “saith” (lxx, Jerome) - as, for example, in <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.14">1Sa 24:14</reference> - affirms that the command is a continuous one. The expression “<hi type="italic">saith your God</hi>” is peculiar to Isaiah, and common to both parts of the collection (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.11">Isa 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.18">Isa 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.10">Isa 33:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa 40:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.21">Isa 41:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.9">Isa 66:9</reference>). The future in all these passages is expressive of that which is taking place or still continuing. And it is the same here. The divine command has not been issued once only, or merely to one prophet, but is being continually addressed to many prophets. “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people,” is the continual charge of the God of the exiles. who has not ceased to be their God even in the midst of wrath, to His messengers and heralds the prophets. <div eID="gen13714" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Appendix to Isaiah</title> <title type="x-s2">Introduction/Exposition of Its Existing State</title> <div sID="gen13715" type="x-p"/> In the commentary on the second half of Isaiah 40-66, I have referred here and there to the expositions of J. Heinemann (Berlin 1842) and Isaiah Hochstädter (Carlsruhe 1827), both written in Hebrew - the former well worthy of notice for criticism of the text, the latter provided with a German translation. For the psalm of Hezekiah (ch. 38) Professor Sam. David Luzzatto of Padua lent me his exposition in manuscript. Since then this great and noble-minded man has departed this life (on the 29th Sept. 1865). His commentary on Isaiah, so far as it has been printed, is full of information and of new and stirring explanations, written in plain, lucid, rabbinical language. It would be a great misfortune for the second half of this valuable work to remain unprinted. I well remember the assistance which the deceased afforded me in my earlier studies of the history of the post-biblical Jewish poetry (1836), and the affection which he displayed when I renewed my former acquaintance with him on the occasion of his publishing his Isaiah; so that I lament his loss on my own account as well as in the interests of science. “Why have you allowed twenty-five years to pass,” he wrote to me on the 22nd Feb. 1863, “without telling me that you remembered me? Is it because we form different opinions of the עלמה and the ילד ילד לנו of Isaiah? Are you a sincere Christian? Then you are a hundred times dearer to me than so many Israelitish scholars, the partizans of Spinoza, with whom our age swarms.” These words indicate very clearly the standpoint taken in his writings. <div eID="gen13715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> Of the commentaries written in English, I am acquainted not only with <hi type="italic">Lowth</hi>, but with the thoroughly practical commentary of <hi type="italic">Henderson</hi> (1857), and that of <hi type="italic">Joseph Addison</hi> <hi type="italic">Alexander</hi>, Prov. in Princeton (1847, etc.), which is very much read as an exegetical repertorium in England also. But I had neither of them in my possession. <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Isa 1:1</reference> <div eID="gen13716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13717" type="x-p"/> What I have said here on <reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Isa 1:1</reference> as the heading to the whole book, or at any rate to Isaiah 1-39, has been said in part by Photios also in his <hi type="italic">Amphilochia</hi>, which Sophocles the M.D. has published complete from a MS of Mount Athos (Athens 1858, 4).  <chapter eID="Isa.40"/> <div eID="gen13717" type="x-p"/>
entries.ffd38b7eea277ea3f38fbf1d9bbd32d3fc834d75: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.2">Isa 40:2</reference> <div eID="gen13318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13319" type="x-p"/> The summons is now repeated with still greater emphasis, the substance of the consoling proclamation being also given. <hi type="italic">“Speak ye to the heart of Jerusalem, and cry unto her, that her affliction is ended, that her debt is paid, that she has received from the hand of Jehovah double for all her sins.”</hi> The holy city is thought of here in connection with the population belonging to it. על־לב דּבּר (to speak to the heart) is an expression applied in <reference osisRef="Gen.34.3">Gen 34:3</reference> and Jdg 19:3 to words adapted to win the heart; in <reference osisRef="Gen.50.21">Gen 50:21</reference>, to the words used by Joseph to inspire his brethren with confidence; whilst here it is used in precisely the same sense as in Hos 2:16, and possibly not without a reminiscence of this earlier prophecy. אל קרא (to call to a person) is applied to a prophetic announcement made to a person, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.7.27">Jer 7:27</reference>; Zec 1:4. The announcement to be made to Jerusalem is then introduced with כּי, ὅτι, which serves as the introduction to either an indirect or a direct address (Ges. §155, 1,<hi type="italic">e</hi>). (1.) Her affliction has become full, and therefore has come to an end. צבא, military service, then feudal service, and hardship generally (<reference osisRef="Job.7.1">Job 7:1</reference>); here it applies to the captivity or exile - that unsheltered bivouac, as it were, of the people who had bee transported into a foreign land, and were living there in bondage, restlessness, and insecurity. (2.) Her iniquity is atoned for, and the justice of God is satisfied: <hi type="italic">nirtsâh</hi>, which generally denotes a satisfactory reception, is used here in the sense of meeting with a satisfactory payment, like עון רצה in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.41">Lev 26:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.43">Lev 26:43</reference>, to pay off the debt of sin by enduring the punishment of sin. (3.) The third clause repeats the substance of the previous ones with greater emphasis and in a fuller tone: Jerusalem has already suffered fully for her sins. In direct opposition to לקחה, which cannot, when connected with two actual perfects as it is here, be take as a perfect used to indicate the certainty of some future occurrence, Gesenius, Hitzig, Ewald, Umbreit, Stier, and Hahn suppose <hi type="italic">kiphlayim</hi> to refer to the double favour that Jerusalem was about to receive (like <hi type="italic">mishneh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.61.7">Isa 61:7</reference>, and possibly borrowed from Isaiah in Zec 9:12), instead of to the double punishment which Jerusalem had endured (like <hi type="italic">mishneh</hi> in <reference osisRef="Jer.16.18">Jer 16:18</reference>). It is not to be taken, however, in a judicial sense; in which case God would appear over-rigid, and therefore unjust. Jerusalem had not suffered more than its sins had deserved; but the compassion of God regarded what His justice had been obliged to inflict upon Jerusalem as superabundant. This compassion also expresses itself in the words “for all” (<hi type="italic">bekhol</hi>, c. <hi type="italic">Beth pretii</hi>): there is nothing left for further punishment. The turning-point from wrath to love has arrived. The wrath has gone forth in double measure. With what intensity, therefore, will the love break forth, which has been so long restrained!
entries.4d89b3c3893045056de17ec8c4b94918a6570813: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference> <div eID="gen13319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13320" type="x-p"/> There is a <hi type="italic">sethume</hi> in the text at this point. The first two vv. form a small <hi type="italic">parashah</hi> by themselves, the prologue of the prologue. After the substance of the consolation has been given on its negative side, the question arises, What positive salvation is to be expected? This question is answered for the prophet, inasmuch as, in the ecstatic stillness of his mind as turned to God, he hears a marvellous voice. <hi type="italic">“Hark, a crier! In the wilderness prepare ye a way for Jehovah, make smooth in the desert a road for our God.”</hi> This is not to be rendered “a voice cries” (Ges., Umbreit, etc.); but the two words are in the construct state, and form an interjectional clause, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.13.4">Isa 13:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.52.8">Isa 52:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.6">Isa 66:6</reference> : Voice of one crying! Who the crier is remains concealed; his person vanishes in the splendour of his calling, and falls into the background behind the substance of his cry. The cry sounds like the long-drawn trumpet-blast of a herald (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.16.1">Isa 16:1</reference>). The crier is like the outrider of a king, who takes care that the way by which the king is to go shall be put into good condition. The king is Jehovah; and it is all the more necessary to prepare the way for Him in a becoming manner, that this way leads through the pathless desert. <hi type="italic">Bammidbâr</hi> is to be connected with <hi type="italic">pannū</hi>, according to the accents on account of the parallel (<hi type="italic">zakeph katan</hi> has a stronger disjunctive force here than <hi type="italic">zekpeh gadol</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.26.14">Deu 26:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.8">Deu 28:8</reference>; 2Ki 1:6), though without any consequent collision with the New Testament description of the fulfilment itself. And so also the Targum and Jewish expositors take במדבר קור קול together, like the lxx, and after this the Gospels. We may, or rather apparently we must, imagine the crier as advancing into the desert, and summoning the people to come and make a road through it. But why does the way of Jehovah lie through the desert, and whither does it lead? It was through the desert that He went to redeem Israel out of Egyptian bondage, and to reveal Himself to Israel from Sinai (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">Deu 33:2</reference>; Jdg 5:4; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.8">Psa 88:8</reference>); and in <reference osisRef="Ps.88.4">Psa 88:4</reference> (5.) God the Redeemer of His people is called <hi type="italic">hârōkhēbh</hi> <hi type="italic">bâ‛ărâbhōth</hi>. Just as His people looked for Him then, when they were between Egypt and Canaan; so was He to be looked for by His people again, now that they were in the “desert of the sea” (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.1">Isa 21:1</reference>), and separated by <hi type="italic">Arabia deserta</hi> from their fatherland. If He were coming at the head of His people, He Himself would clear the hindrances out of His way; but He was coming through the desert to Israel, and therefore Israel itself was to take care that nothing should impede the rapidity or detract from the favour of the Coming One. The description answers to the reality; but, as we shall frequently find as we go further on, the literal meaning spiritualizes itself in an allegorical way.
entries.0e914f7cbf8d2761332c2924d6a478c9a1ddb196: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.4">Isa 40:4</reference> <div eID="gen13320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13321" type="x-p"/> The summons proceeds in a commanding tone. <hi type="italic">“Let every valley be exalted, and every mountain and hill made low; and let the rugged be made a plain, and the ledges of rocks a valley.”</hi> והיה, which takes its tone from the two jussive verbs, is also itself equivalent to ויהי. Instead of גּיא (from גּיא), the pointing in Zec 14:4, we have here (according to Kimchi) the vowel-pointing גּיא; at the same time, the editions of Brescia, Pesaro, Venice 1678, have גּיא (with <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>), and this is also the reading of a codex of Luzzatto without Masoretic notes. The command, according to its spiritual interpretation, points to the encouragement of those that are cast down, the humiliation of the self-righteous and self-secure, the changing of dishonesty into simplicity, and of unapproachable haughtiness into submission (for <hi type="italic">‛âqōbh</hi>, hilly, rugged,<note placement="foot">In this ethical sense Essex applied the word to Queen Elizabeth. See Hefele, <hi type="italic">Ximenes,</hi> p. 90 (ed. 2).</note> compare <reference osisRef="Jer.17.9">Jer 17:9</reference> together with <reference osisRef="Hab.2.4">Hab 2:4</reference>). In general, the meaning is that Israel is to take care, that the God who is coming to deliver it shall find it in such an inward and outwards state as befits His exaltation and His purpose.
entries.f4d31529373395966ddbd402c618fd9d719ea649: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Isa 40:5</reference> <div eID="gen13321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13322" type="x-p"/> The cry of the crier proceeds thus in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Isa 40:5</reference> : <hi type="italic">“And the glory of Jehovah will be revealed, and all flesh seeth together: for the mouth of Jehovah hath spoken it.”</hi> The pret. cons. קנגלה is here <hi type="italic">apodosis imper</hi>. When the way is prepared for Jehovah the Coming One, the glory of the God of salvation will unveil itself (on the name <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi>, which is applied to God, the absolute I, as living and revealing Himself in history, more especially in the history of salvation). His <hi type="italic">parousia</hi> is the revelation of His glory (1Pe 4:13). This revelation is made for the good of Israel, but not secretly or exclusively; for all the human race, called here designedly “all flesh” (<hi type="italic">kol</hi> <hi type="italic">bâsâr</hi>), will come to see it (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.3.6">Luk 3:6</reference>, “the salvation of God”). Man, because he is flesh, cannot see God without dying (<reference osisRef="Exod.33.20">Exo 33:20</reference>); but the future will fill up this gulf of separation. The object to the verb “see” is not what follows, as Rosenmüller supposes, viz., “that the mouth of Jehovah hath spoken,” for the word of promise which is here fulfilled is not one addressed to all flesh; nor does it mean, “see that Jehovah hath spoken with His own mouth,” i.e., after having become man, as Stier maintains, for the verb required in this case would be מדבּר, not דּבּר. The clause, “for the mouth of Jehovah hath spoken it,” is rather Isaiah’s usual confirmation of the foregoing prophecy. Here the crier uses it to establish the certainty of what he foretells, provided that Israel will do what he summons it to perform.
entries.8648b41e5bf2124633931a39ee8949953f5b0ba6: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.6-Isa.40.8">Isa 40:6-8</reference> <div eID="gen13322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13323" type="x-p"/> The prophet now hears a second voice, and then a third, entering into conversation with it. <hi type="italic">“Hark, one speaking, Cry! And he answers, What shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and all its beauty as the flower of the field. Grass is withered, flower faded: for the breath of Jehovah has blown upon it. Surely grass is the people; grass withereth, flower fadeth: yet the word of our God will stand for ever.”</hi> A second voice celebrates the divine word of promise in the face of the approaching fulfilment, and appoints a preacher of its eternal duration. The verb is not ואמר (<hi type="italic">et dixi</hi>, lxx, Vulg.), but ואמר; so that the person asking the question is not the prophet himself, but an ideal person, whom he has before him in visionary objectiveness. The appointed theme of his proclamation is the perishable nature of all flesh (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.5">Isa 40:5</reference> πᾶσα σάρξ, here πᾶσα ἡ σάρξ), and, on the other hand, the imperishable nature of the word of God. Men living in the flesh are universally impotent, perishing, limited; God, on the contrary (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">Isa 31:3</reference>), is the omnipotent, eternal, all-determining; and like Himself, so is His word, which, regarded as the vehicle and utterance of His willing and thinking, is not something separate from Himself, and therefore is the same as He. <hi type="italic">Chasdō</hi> is the charm or gracefulness of the outward appearance (lxx; 1Pe 1:24, δόξα: see Schott on the passage, Jam 1:11, εὐπρέπεια). The comparison instituted with grass and flower recals <reference osisRef="Isa.37.27">Isa 37:27</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.8.12">Job 8:12</reference>, and still more <reference osisRef="Ps.90.5-Ps.90.6">Psa 90:5-6</reference>, and Job 14:2. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.40.7">Isa 40:7</reference></hi> describes what happens to the grass and flower. The preterites, like the Greek <hi type="italic">aoristus gnomicus</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.26.10">Isa 26:10</reference>), express a fact of experience sustained by innumerable examples: <hi type="italic">exaruit</hi> <hi type="italic">gramen</hi>, <hi type="italic">emarcuit</hi> <hi type="italic">flos</hi>;<note placement="foot">נבל has <hi type="italic">munach</hi> here and in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.8">Isa 40:8</reference> attached to the penultimate in all correct texts (hence <hi type="italic">milel</hi>, on account of the monosyllable which follows), and <hi type="italic">mehteg</hi> on the <hi type="italic">tzere</hi> to sustain the lengthening.</note> consequently the כּי which follows is not hypothetical (granting that), but explanatory of the reason, viz., “because <hi type="italic">rūăch Jehovah</hi> hath blown upon it,” i.e., the “breath” of God the Creator, which pervades the creation, generating life, sustaining life, and destroying life, and whose most characteristic elementary manifestation is the wind. Every breath of wind is a drawing of the breath of the whole life of nature, the active indwelling principle of whose existence is the <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi> of God. A fresh v. ought to commence now with אכן. The clause העם חציר אכן is genuine, and thoroughly in Isaiah’s style, notwithstanding the lxx, which Gesenius and Hitzig follow. עכן is not equivalent to a comparative כן (Ewald, §105,<hi type="italic">a</hi>), but is assuring, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.45.15">Isa 45:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Isa 53:4</reference>; and <hi type="italic">hâ‛âm</hi> (the people) refers to men generally, as in Isa 42:5. The order of thought is in the form of a triolet. The explanation of the striking simile commences with <hi type="italic">'âkhēn</hi> (surely); and then in the repetition of the words, “grass withereth, flower fadeth,” the men are intended, resemble the grass and the flower. Surely grass is the human race; such grass withereth and such flower fadeth, but the word of our God (Jehovah, the God of His people and of sacred history) <hi type="italic">yâqūm</hi> <hi type="italic">le‛ōlâm</hi>, i.e., it rises up without withering or fading, and endures for ever, fulfilling and verifying itself through all times. This general truth refers, in the preset instance, to the word of promise uttered by the voice in the desert. If the word of God generally has an eternal duration, more especially is this the case with the word of the <hi type="italic">parousia</hi> of God the Redeemer, the word in which all the words of God are yea and amen. The imperishable nature of this word, however, has for its dark foil the perishable nature of all flesh, and all the beauty thereof. The oppressors of Israel are mortal, and their chesed with which they impose and bribe is perishable; but the word of God, with which Israel can console itself, preserves the fields, and ensures it a glorious end to its history. Thus the seal, which the first crier set upon the promise of Jehovah’s speedy coming, is inviolable; and the comfort which the prophets of God are to bring to His people, who have now been suffering so long, is infallibly sure.
entries.556ce3f1d5c5d7f1183323cfaf566be2c0905df4: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.9">Isa 40:9</reference> <div eID="gen13323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13324" type="x-p"/> The prophet accordingly now takes, as his standpoint, the time when Jehovah will already have come. <hi type="italic">“Upon a high mountain get thee up, O evangelistess Zion; lift up they voice with strength, evangelistess Jerusalem: lift up, be not afraid; say to the cities of Judah, Behold your God.”</hi> Knobel and others follow the lxx and Targum, and regard Zion and Jerusalem as accusatives of the object, viz., “preacher of salvation (i.e., a chorus of preachers) to Zion-Jerusalem;” but such parallels as <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Isa 52:7</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.62.11">Isa 62:11</reference> are misleading here. The words are in apposition (A. S. Th. εὐαγγελιζομένη Σιών). Zion-Jerusalem herself is called an evangelistess: the personification as a female renders this probable at the outset, and it is placed beyond all doubt by the fact, that it is the cities of Judah (the daughters of Zion-Jerusalem) that are to be evangelized. The prophet’s standpoint here is in the very midst of the <hi type="italic">parousia</hi>. When Jerusalem shall have her God in the midst of her once more, after He has broken up His home there for so long a time; she is then, as the restored mother-community, to ascend a high mountain, and raising her voice with fearless strength, to bring to her daughters the joyful news of the appearance of their God. The verb <hi type="italic">bissēr</hi> signifies literally to smooth, to unfold, then to make glad, more especially with joyful news.<note placement="foot">The verb <hi type="italic">bissēr</hi> signifies primarily to stroke, rub, shave, or scratch the surface of anything; then to stroke off or rub off the surface, or anything which covers it; then, suggested by the idea of “rubbing smooth” (<hi type="italic">glatt</hi>), “to smooth a person” (<hi type="italic">jemanden glätten</hi>; compare the English, <hi type="italic">to gladden</hi> a person), i.e., <hi type="italic">vultum ejus diducere</hi>, to make him friendly and cheerful, or “to look smoothly upon a person,” i.e., to show him a friendly face; and also as an intransitive, “<hi type="italic">to be glad</hi>,” to be friendly and cheerful; and lastly, in a general sense, <hi type="italic">aliquid attingere</hi>, <hi type="italic">tractare</hi>, <hi type="italic">attrectare</hi>, to grasp or handle a thing (from which comes <hi type="italic">bâsâr</hi>, the flesh, as something tangible or material). In harmony with the Hebrew <hi type="italic">bissēr</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.15">Jer 20:15</reference>), they say in Arabic <hi type="italic">basarahu</hi> (or intensive, <hi type="italic">bassarahu</hi>) <hi type="italic">bi</hi>-<hi type="italic">maulûdin</hi>, he has gladdened him with the news of the birth of a son.</note> <div eID="gen13324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13325" type="x-p"/> It lies at the root of the New Testament εὐαγγελίζειν (evangelize), and is a favourite word of the author of chapters 40-66, that Old Testament evangelist, though it is no disproof of Isaiah’s authorship (cf., <reference osisRef="Nah.2.1">Nah 2:1</reference>). Hitherto Jerusalem has been in despair, bowed down under the weight of the punishment of her sins, and standing in need of consolation. But now that she has Jehovah with her again, she is to lift up her voice with the most joyful confidence, without further anxiety, and to become, according to her true vocation, the messenger of good tidings to all Judaea.
entries.e873c2dc9344fdeedc28bc7abe5ca571720fcf5c: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Isa 40:10</reference> <div eID="gen13325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13326" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Isa 40:10</reference> the prophet goes back from the standpoint of the fulfilment to that of the prophecy. <hi type="italic">“Behold the Lord, Jehovah, as a mighty one will He come, His arm ruling for Him; behold, His reward is with Him, and His retribution before Him.”</hi> We must not render the first clause “with strong,” i.e., with strength, as the lxx and Targum do. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Isa 26:4</reference>; Ges. §154, 3,<hi type="italic">a</hi>). He will come in the essence, strength, and energy of a strong one; and this is still further defined by the participial, circumstantial clause, “His arm ruling for Him” (<hi type="italic">brachio suo ipsi dominante</hi>). It is His arm that rules for Him, i.e., that either brings into subjection to Him, or else overthrows whatever opposes Him. Nevertheless, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Isa 40:10</reference></hi> does not present Him merely in one aspect, namely as coming to judge and punish, but in both aspects, viz., that of the law and that of the gospel, as a righteous rewarder; hence the double name of God, <hi type="italic">Adonai Jehovah</hi> (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.3.15">Isa 3:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.15">Isa 30:15</reference>, all in the first part), which is used even in the Pentateuch, and most frequently by Amos and Ezekiel, and which forms, as it were, an anagram. פּעלּה is already met with in <reference osisRef="Lev.19.13">Lev 19:13</reference> as a synonym of שׂכר, passing from the general idea of <hi type="italic">work</hi> to that of something earned and forfeited. Jehovah brings with Him the penal reward of the enemies of His people, and also the gracious reward of the faithful of His people, whom He will compensate for their previous sufferings with far exceeding joys (see <reference osisRef="Isa.62.11">Isa 62:11</reference>).
entries.028fdc2cd7be9e05aa222c3d16c90061247638a8: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Isa 40:11</reference> <div eID="gen13326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13327" type="x-p"/> The prophet dwells upon this, the redeeming side not the judicial, as he proceeds to place the image of the good shepherd by the side of that of the Lord Jehovah. <hi type="italic">“He will feed His flock like a shepherd, take the lambs in His arm, and carry them in His bosom, and gently lead those that are giving suck.”</hi> The flock is His people, now dispersed in a foreign land. The love with which He tends this flock is shown, by way of example, in His conduct towards the טלאים (= טליים from טלי = טלה), the young lambs that have not long been born, and the עלות, those giving suck, <hi type="italic">lactantes</hi> (Vulg. <hi type="italic">fetae</hi>), not those that are sucking, <hi type="italic">sugentes</hi> (from עוּל <hi type="italic">med. Vav</hi>, to nourish). Such as cannot keep pace with the flock he takes in his arms, and carries in the bosom of his dress; and the mothers he does not overdrive, but ינהל (see at <reference osisRef="Ps.23.2">Psa 23:2</reference>), lets them go gently alone, because they require care (<reference osisRef="Gen.33.13">Gen 33:13</reference>). With this loving picture the prologue in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1-Isa.40.11">Isa 40:1-11</reference> is brought to a close. It stands at the head of the whole, like a divine inauguration of the prophet, and like the quintessence of what he is commanded to proclaim. Nevertheless it is also an integral part of the first address. For the questions which follow cannot possibly be the commencement of the prophecy, though it is not very clear how far they form a continuation. <div eID="gen13327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13328" type="x-p"/> The connection is the following: The prophet shows both didactically and paraenetically what kind of God it is whose appearance to redeem His people has been prophetically announced in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.1">Isa 40:1</reference>-11. He is the incomparably exalted One. This incomparable exaltation makes the ignorance of the worshipers of idols the more apparent, but it serves to comfort Israel. And Israel needs such consolation in its present banishment, in which it is so hard for it to comprehend the ways of God.
entries.382387131f65d10449d702c81c36ff018cabbdf3: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa 40:12</reference> <div eID="gen13328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13329" type="x-p"/> In order to bring His people to the full consciousness of the exaltation of Jehovah, the prophet asks in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa 40:12</reference>, <hi type="italic">“Who hath measured the waters with the hollow of his hand, and regulated the heavens with a span, and taken up the dust of the earth in a third measure, and weighed the mountains with a steelyard, and hills with balances?”</hi> Jehovah, and He alone, has given to all these their proper quantities, their determinate form, and their proportionate place in the universe. How very little can a man hold in the hollow of his hand (<hi type="italic">shō‛al</hi>)!<note placement="foot">The root שׁל, Arab. <hi type="italic">sl</hi> has the primary meaning of easily moving or being easily moved; then of being loose or slack, of hanging down, or sinking-a meaning which we meet with in שׁעל and שׁאל. Accordingly, <hi type="italic">shō‛al</hi> signifies the palm (i.e., the depression made by the hand), and <hi type="italic">she'ōl</hi> not literally a hollowing or cavity, but a depression or low ground.</note> how very small is the space which a man’s span will cover! how little is contained in the third of an ephah (<hi type="italic">shâlı̄sh</hi>; see at <reference osisRef="Ps.80.6">Psa 80:6</reference>)! and how trifling in either bulk or measure is the quantity you can weight in scales, whether it be a <hi type="italic">peles</hi>, i.e., a steelyard (<hi type="italic">statera</hi>), or <hi type="italic">mō'zenayim</hi>, a tradesman’s balance (<hi type="italic">bilances</hi>), consisting of two scales.<note placement="foot">According to the meaning, to level or equalize, which is one meaning of <hi type="italic">pillēs</hi>, the noun <hi type="italic">peles</hi> is applied not only to a level used to secure equilibrium, which is called <hi type="italic">mishqeleth</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.17">Isa 28:17</reference>, but also to a steelyard used for weighing, the beam of which consists of a lever with unequal arms, which flies up directly the weight is removed.</note> <div eID="gen13329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13330" type="x-p"/> But what Jehovah measures with the hollow of His hand, and with His span, is nothing less than the waters beneath and the heavens above. He carries a scoop, in which there is room for all the dust of which the earth consists, and a scale on which He has weighed the great colossal mountains.
entries.934c67a917bd487555abadb21f42f30313fb1bcb: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.13-Isa.40.14">Isa 40:13-14</reference> <div eID="gen13330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13331" type="x-p"/> A second question follows in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Isa 40:13</reference>, Isa 40:14. <hi type="italic">“Who regulated the Spirit of Jehovah, and </hi>(<hi type="italic">who</hi>)<hi type="italic">instructed Him as His counsellor? With whom took He counsel, and who would have explained to Him and instructed Him concerning the path of right, and taught Him knowledge, and made known to Him a prudent course?”</hi> The first question called to mind the omnipotence of Jehovah; this recalls His omniscience, which has all fulness in itself, and therefore precludes all instruction from without. “The Spirit of Jehovah” is the Spirit which moved upon the waters at the creation, and by which chaos was reduced to order. “Who,” inquires this prophet - “who furnished this Spirit with the standard, according to which all this was to be done?” תּכּן as in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12">Isa 40:12</reference>, to bring into conformity with rule, and so to fit for regulated working. Instead of <hi type="italic">mercha tifchah athnach</hi>, which suggests the Targum rendering, “<hi type="italic">quis direxit spiritum? Jehova</hi>” (vid., <reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference>), it would be more correct to adopt the accentuation <hi type="italic">tifchah munach athnach</hi> (cf., <reference osisRef="Exod.21.24">Exo 21:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.23.9">Exo 23:9</reference>), and there are certain codices in which we find this (see Dachselt). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Isa 40:13</reference></hi> we might follow the Septuagint translation, καὶ τίς αὐτοῦ σύμβουλος ἐγένετο ὃς σύμβιβᾶ (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Rom 11:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.16">1Co 2:16</reference>, συμβιβάσει) αὐτόν, but in this case we miss the verb היה. The rendering we have given above is not so harsh, and the accentuation is indifferent here, since <hi type="italic">silluk</hi> is never written without <hi type="italic">tifchah</hi>if only a single word precedes it. In <reference osisRef="Isa.40.14">Isa 40:14</reference> the reciprocal נוע is connected with את = אם. The <hi type="italic">futt. cons.</hi> retain their literal meaning: with whom did He consult, so that he supplied Him with understanding in consequence (<hi type="italic">hēbhı̄n</hi>, generally to understand, here in a causative sense). The verbs of instruction are sometimes construed with בּ of the lesson taught, sometimes with a double accusative. In reply to the questions in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Isa 40:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.14">Isa 40:14</reference>, which are essentially one, Israel must acknowledge that its God is the possessor of absolute might, and also of absolute wisdom.
entries.8d3d9edbff3c3dccca10688edcfb7773004cb9ab: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Isa 40:15</reference> <div eID="gen13331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13332" type="x-p"/> From His exaltation as Creator, the prophet now proceeds to His exaltation as Governor of the world. <hi type="italic">“Behold, nations like a little drop on a bucket, and like a grain of sand in a balance, are they esteemed; behold, islands like an atom of dust that rises in the air.”</hi> Upon Jehovah, the King of the world, does the burden rest of ruling over the whole human race, which is split up into different nations; but the great masses of people over whom Jehovah rules are no more burden to Him than a drop hanging upon a bucket is a burden to the man who carries it (<hi type="italic">min</hi> is used in the same sense as in Sol 4:1; Sol 6:5), no more than the weight in a balance is perceptibly increased or diminished by a grain of sand that happens to lie upon it (<hi type="italic">shachaq</hi>, from <hi type="italic">shâchaq</hi>, to grind to powder). The <hi type="italic">islands</hi>, those fragments of firm ground in the midst of the ocean (אי = <hi type="italic">ivy</hi>, from אוה, to betake one’s self to a place, and remain there), upon which the heathen world was dispersed (Gen 10), are to Him who carries the universe like the small particle of dust (דּק from דּקק, to crush or pulverize), which is lifted up, viz., by the slightest breath of wind (יטּול metaplastic <hi type="italic">fut. niph.</hi> of <hi type="italic">tūl</hi> = <hi type="italic">nâtal</hi>, cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Isa 63:9</reference>). The rendering of Knobel, “dust which is thrown,” would require עפר (<reference osisRef="Isa.41.2">Isa 41:2</reference>); and neither that of Gesenius, viz., “He takes up islands like a particle of dust,” nor that of Hitzig, “He carries islands,” etc., is admissible, for טוּל = נטל signifies <hi type="italic">tollere</hi>, not <hi type="italic">portare</hi>; and the former, viz., <hi type="italic">insulas tollit</hi>, furnishes no answer to the question, “How so, and to what end?”
entries.1d402fbc869c7ba1eb3ab3199a0f32027e451ac0: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.16">Isa 40:16</reference> <div eID="gen13332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13333" type="x-p"/> By the side of this vanishing diminutiveness on the part of man as contrasted with Jehovah, everything by which man could express his adoration of the exalted One comes incomparably short of His exaltation. <hi type="italic">“And Lebanon is not a sufficiency of burning, nor its game a sufficiency of burnt-offerings;”</hi> i.e., there is not enough wood to sustain the fire, nor a sufficient supply of sacrificial animals to be slaughtered, and to ascend in fire. דּי (constr. דּי) signifies that which suffices (and then that which is plentiful); it differs therefore from τὸ δέον, what is requisite.<note placement="foot">The derivation of דּי is still more obscure than that of δεῖ, which signifies, according to Benfey (<hi type="italic">Wurzelwörterbuch</hi>, ii. 205), “there needs;” according to Sonne, “it binds, scil. ἡ ἀνάγκη.”</note>
entries.24fc7db653debe3fb719a69122f4a86eb93d4186: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.17">Isa 40:17</reference> <div eID="gen13333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13334" type="x-p"/> From the obverse of the thought in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Isa 40:15</reference> the prophet returns to the thought itself, and dwells upon it still further. <hi type="italic">“All the nations are as nothing before Him; they are regarded by Him as belonging to nullity and emptiness.”</hi> <hi type="italic">'Ephes</hi> is the end at which a thing ceases, and in an absolute sense that at which all being ceases, hence non-existence or nullity. <hi type="italic">Tōhū</hi> (from <hi type="italic">tâhâh</hi>, related to <hi type="italic">shâ'âh</hi>; vid., <hi type="italic">Comm. on Job</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Job.37.6">Job 37:6</reference>), a horrible desolation, like the chaos of creation, where there is nothing definite, and therefore as good as nothing at all; <hi type="italic">min</hi> is hardly comparative in the sense of “more nothing than nothing itself” (Like <reference osisRef="Job.11.17">Job 11:17</reference>, where “brighter” is to be supplied, or Mic 7:4, where “sharper” is similarly required), but is used in the same partitive sense as in <reference osisRef="Isa.41.24">Isa 41:24</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.44.11">Isa 44:11</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.62.10">Psa 62:10</reference>).
entries.3958b68038325e347cb59009eb0629678332d7cc: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">Isa 40:18</reference> <div eID="gen13334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13335" type="x-p"/> The conclusion drawn from <reference osisRef="Isa.40.17">Isa 40:17</reference>, that Jehovah is therefore the matchless Being, shapes itself into a question, which is addressed not to idolaters, but to such of the Israelites as needed to be armed against the seductive power of idolatry, to which the majority of mankind had yielded. <hi type="italic">“And to whom can ye liken God, and what kind of image can ye place beside Him!”</hi> The ו before ואל is conclusive, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.26">Isa 28:26</reference>, and the futures are modi potent.: with what can ye bring into comparison (אל as in <reference osisRef="Isa.14.10">Isa 14:10</reference>) <hi type="italic">El</hi>, i.e., God, the one Being who is absolutely the Mighty? and what kind of <hi type="italic">demūth</hi> (i.e., divine, like Himself) can ye place by His side?
entries.86737ed084c3d00624615f27180579b350b0f980: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.19">Isa 40:19</reference> <div eID="gen13335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13336" type="x-p"/> Least of all can an idol bear comparison with Him. <hi type="italic">“The idol, when the smith has cast it, the melter plates it with gold, and melteth silver chains for it.”</hi> The object (<hi type="italic">happesel</hi>, the idol), which is here placed first as the theme in the accusative (lit. the image hewn out), denotes in this instance an idol generally. חרשׁ is as comprehensive as <hi type="italic">faber</hi>. בּזּהב רקּע signifies here to cover over with a זהב רקּע (<hi type="italic">laminâ auri</hi>), the verb being used in a denominative sense, and not in its primary meaning. As we must assume, according to <reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">Isa 40:20</reference>, that the prophet intends to carry us into the midst of the process of manufacturing the idol, the paratactic expression is to be pointed as above, viz., “after the (a) smith has cast it (compare Arab. <hi type="italic">nasik</hi>, a piece of cast metal), the (a) melter (goldsmith) covers it with gold plate;” and <hi type="italic">tsōrēph</hi>, which is palindromically repeated, according to Isaiah’s custom, is not the third pers. <hi type="italic">poel</hi> (on the <hi type="italic">poel</hi> of strong stems, see at <reference osisRef="Job.9.15">Job 9:15</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.109.10">Psa 109:10</reference>), but a participle, equivalent to הוּא צורף (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.8">Isa 29:8</reference>, which see; and also, according to the accents, <reference osisRef="Isa.33.5">Isa 33:5</reference>), “and he melteth chains of silver,” viz., to fasten the image.
entries.c5294c8cd69609ef0fc81903d8ce4dea9bea36f5: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">Isa 40:20</reference> <div eID="gen13336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13337" type="x-p"/> This is the origin of a metal idol. The wooden idol is described in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.20">Isa 40:20</reference> : <hi type="italic">“The man who is impoverished in oblations, he chooseth a block of wood that will not rot; he seeketh for himself a skilful smith, to prepare an idol that will not shake.”</hi> He who has fallen into such poverty that he can only offer to his God a poor oblation (<hi type="italic">terūmâh</hi>, accusative, according to Ewald, §284,<hi type="italic">c</hi>), has an idol cut for himself out of a block of wood. That <hi type="italic">sâkhan</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">sakana</hi> or <hi type="italic">sakuna</hi>)<note placement="foot">Both forms occur in this sense, according to the evidence of original sources, with the common imperative <hi type="italic">yaskunu</hi>, the infinitive <hi type="italic">sukūne</hi> passed over by Freytag, the verbal substantive <hi type="italic">maskane</hi>, and the adjective <hi type="italic">miskin</hi> or <hi type="italic">meskin</hi>, primarily to be forced to inactivity through weakness, destitution, or outward influences, not to be able to move and exert one’s self; or, more particularly, not to be able to defend one’s self (as it were to be obliged to sit still or keep still). Hence more especially <hi type="italic">opibus et facultatibus carens</hi>, being in distress, destitute, poor.</note> is an ancient word, is evident from Deu 8:9. The verb <hi type="italic">yimmōt</hi>, like <hi type="italic">yittōl</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Isa 40:15</reference>, is a fut. <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, to be made to shake. A wooden image, which is planed at the bottom, and made heavier below than above, to prevent its falling over with every shock, is to be a god! The thing carries its own satire, even when described with the greatest seriousness.
entries.f315579d2b6386045ebd5234758f74a068214ee4: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.21">Isa 40:21</reference> <div eID="gen13337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13338" type="x-p"/> Having thus depicted in a few strokes the infatuation of idolatry, the prophet addresses the following question to such of the Israelites as are looking at it with longing eye, even if they have not already been deluded by it. <hi type="italic">“Do ye not know? Do ye not hear? Is it not proclaimed to you from the beginning? Have ye not obtained an insight into the foundations of the earth?”</hi> We have here four questions chiastically arranged. The absolute being of God, which is above all created things, is something which may be either inferred <hi type="italic">per ratiocinationem</hi>, or learned <hi type="italic">per traditionem</hi>. When Israel failed to acknowledge the absolute distinctness and unequalled supremacy of Jehovah its God, it hardened itself against the knowledge which it might acquire even in a natural way (cf., <reference osisRef="Ps.19.1-Ps.19.14">Psa 19:1-14</reference> and <reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Rom 1:20</reference>), and shut its ears against the teaching of revelation and tradition, which had come down from the very beginning of its history. The first two questions are construed with futures, the other two with perfects; the former refer to what is possible, the latter to what is an actual fact. Have you - this is the meaning of the four questions - have you obtained no knowledge of the foundations of the earth, namely, as to the way in which they were laid?
entries.861f9a0b3f4b102c71ba804120165693398a2ba2: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Isa 40:22</reference> <div eID="gen13338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13339" type="x-p"/> The prophet now proceeds to describe the God whom both His works and word proclaim. The participles which follow are predicates of the subject, which filled the consciousness of the prophet as well as that of every believer. <hi type="italic">“He who is enthroned above the vault of the earth, and its inhabitants resemble grasshoppers; who has spread out the heavens like gauze, and stretched them out like a tent-roof to dwell in.”</hi> He, the manifested and yet unknown, is He who has for His throne the circle of the heavens (<hi type="italic">chūg shâmayim</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.22.14">Job 22:14</reference>), which arches over the earth, and to whom from His inaccessible height men appear as diminutive as grasshoppers (Num 13:33); He who has spread out the blue sky like a thin transparent garment (<hi type="italic">dōq</hi>, a thin fabric, like <hi type="italic">daq</hi>, fine dust, in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Isa 40:15</reference>), and stretched it out above the earth like a tent for dwelling in (<hi type="italic">'ōhel</hi><note placement="foot">The noun <hi type="italic">'ōhel</hi> is derived from the root אל, from which come Arab. <hi type="italic">'wl</hi>, <hi type="italic">coaluit</hi>, <hi type="italic">cohaesit</hi>, to thicken within or gain consistency (hence, regarded on another side, to lose in outward extent or outward bulk, to shrink; to go back to its original or essential condition; to issue in something as the final result; or generally, to draw back or return from a distance), and Arab. <hi type="italic">'h'</hi>, to attach one’s self or accustom one’s self to a person or thing, equivalent to <hi type="italic">alifa</hi> and <hi type="italic">anisa</hi>; to take up one’s abode in a place, or absolutely, to commence housekeeping by marrying, like the Italian <hi type="italic">accasarsi</hi>, Turkish <hi type="italic">ewlenmek</hi> (from <hi type="italic">ew</hi>, a house); or, when applied to a place itself, to be habitable, inhabited, and cultivated (= pass. <hi type="italic">uhila</hi>, more especially in the participle <hi type="italic">âhil</hi>, = <hi type="italic">‛âmir</hi> = <hi type="italic">ma‛mūr</hi>). (Hence <hi type="italic">ahl</hi>, one who belongs to a person or place, with its numerous applications, and also אהל, a tent (primarily a dwelling generally, Engl. <hi type="italic">abode</hi>), which stands at the end of this etymological series.</note><hi type="italic">lâshebheth</hi>). The participle brings to view the actions and circumstances of all times. In the present instance, where it is continued in the historical sense, it is to be resolved into the perfect; in other cases, the preservation of the world is evidently thought of as a <hi type="italic">creatio continua</hi> (see <hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> P. 111).
entries.50c66e5c6cf9adb028a13aea24129adf1dd8822a: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.23-Isa.40.24">Isa 40:23-24</reference> <div eID="gen13339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13340" type="x-p"/> This is followed by a series of predicates of God the Ruler of the universe. <hi type="italic">“He who giveth up rulers to annihilation; maketh judges of the earth like a desolation. They are hardly planted, hardly sown, their stem has hardly taken root in the earth, and He only blows upon them, and they dry up, and the storm carries them away like stubble.”</hi> There is nothing so high and inaccessible in the world, that He cannot bring it to nothing, even in the midst of its most self-confident and threatening exaltation. <hi type="italic">Rōzenı̄m</hi> are solemn persons, σεμνοί, possessors of the greatest distinction and influence; <hi type="italic">shōphelı̄m</hi>, those who combine in themselves the highest judicial and administrative power. The former He gives up to annihilation; the latter He brings into a condition resembling the negative state of the <hi type="italic">tōhū</hi> out of which the world was produced, and to which it can be reduced again. We are reminded here of such descriptions as <reference osisRef="Job.12.17">Job 12:17</reference>, Job 12:24. The suddenness of the catastrophe is depicted in Isa 40:24. אף בּל (which only occurs here), when followed by וגם in the apodosis (cf., 2Ki 20:4), signifies that even this has not yet taken place when the other also occurs: hence <hi type="italic">vixdum plantati sunt</hi>, etc. The <hi type="italic">niphal</hi> נטּע and the <hi type="italic">pual</hi> זרע denote the hopeful commencement; the <hi type="italic">poel</hi>שׁרשׁ the hopeful continuation. A layer or seed excites the hope of blossom and fruit, more especially when it has taken root; but nothing more is needed than a breath of Jehovah, and it is all over with it (the verb <hi type="italic">nâshaph</hi> is used in this verse, where plants with stems are referred to; a verb with a softer labial, <hi type="italic">nâshabh</hi>, was employed above in connection with grass and flowers). A single withering breath lays them at rest; and by the power of Jehovah there rises a stormy wind, which carries them away like light dry stubble (נשׂא); compare, on the other hand, the verb used in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.15">Isa 40:15</reference>, viz., <hi type="italic">tūl</hi> = <hi type="italic">nâtal</hi>, to lift up, to keep in the air).
entries.a56844e6dcdaafb0682ea016e2324574a0ea44ee: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa 40:25</reference> <div eID="gen13340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13341" type="x-p"/> The thought of <reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">Isa 40:18</reference> now recurs like a refrain, a conclusion being appended to the premises by means of ו, as was the case there. <hi type="italic">“And to whom will ye compare me, to whom I can be equal? saith the Holy One.”</hi> Not <hi type="italic">haqqâdōsh</hi>, because a poetical or oratorical style omits the article wherever it can be dispensed with. The Holy One asks this, and can ask it, because as such He is also exalted above the whole world (<reference osisRef="Job.15.15">Job 15:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.25.5">Job 25:5</reference>).
entries.8d522283baefa32733ea454207a0a367ed599e5a: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.26">Isa 40:26</reference> <div eID="gen13341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13342" type="x-p"/> After the questions in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.18">Isa 40:18</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa 40:25</reference>, which close syllogistically, a third start is made, to demonstrate the incomparable nature of Jehovah. <hi type="italic">“Lift up your eyes on high, and see: who hath created these things? It is He who bringeth out their host by number, calleth them all by names, because of the greatness of </hi>(<hi type="italic">His</hi>)<hi type="italic">might, and as being strong in power: there is not one that is missing.”</hi> Jehovah spoke in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa 40:25</reference>; now the prophet speaks again. We have here the same interchange which occurs in every prophetic book from Deuteronomy downwards, and in which the divine fulness of the prophets is displayed. The answer does not begin with המּוציא, in the sense of “He who brings them out has created them;” but the participle is the predicate to the subject of which the prophet’s soul is full: Jehovah, it is He who brings out the army of stars upon the plane of heaven, as a general leads out his army upon the field of battle, and that <hi type="italic">bemispâr</hi>, by number, counting the innumerable stars, those children of light in armour of light, which meet the eye as it looks up by night. The finite verb יקרא denotes that which takes place every night. He calls them all by name (comp. the derivative passage, <reference osisRef="Ps.147.4">Psa 147:4</reference>): this He does on account of the greatness and fulness of His might (<hi type="italic">'ōnı̄m</hi>, <hi type="italic">vires</hi>, <hi type="italic">virtus</hi>), and as strong in power, i.e., because He is so. This explanation is simpler than Ewald’s (§293,<hi type="italic">c</hi>), viz., “because of the power (τὸ κρατερὸν) of the Strong One.” The call addressed to the stars that are to rise is the call of the Almighty, and therefore not one of all the innumerable host remains behind. אישׁ individualizes; נעדּר (participle), as in <reference osisRef="Isa.34.16">Isa 34:16</reference>, suggests the idea of a sheep that is missed from the flock through staying behind. The second part of the address closes here, having demonstrated the folly of idolatry from the infinite superiority of God; and from this the third part deduces consolation for Israel in the midst of its despair.
entries.0375b7e77b8d93b856fa487f859830f6009c9af4: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.27">Isa 40:27</reference> <div eID="gen13342" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13343" type="x-p"/> Such of the Israelites are required first of all to be brought to a consciousness of the folly of idolatry are not called Israel at all, because they place themselves on a part with the <hi type="italic">gōyı̄m</hi>. But now the prophet addresses those of little faith, who nevertheless desire salvation; those who are cast down, but not in utter despair. <hi type="italic">“Why sayest thou, O Jacob, and speakest, O Israel, My way is hidden from Jehovah, and my right is overlooked by my God?”</hi> The name <hi type="italic">Jacob</hi> stands here at the head, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.29.22">Isa 29:22</reference>, as being the more exquisite name, and the one which more immediately recalled their patriarchal ancestor. They fancied that Jehovah had completely turned away from them in wrath and weariness. “My way” refers to their thorny way of life; “my right” (<hi type="italic">mishpâtı̄</hi>) to their good right, in opposition to their oppressors. Of all this He appeared to take no notice at all. He seemed to have no thought of vindicating it judicially (on the double min, away from him, see Ges. §154, 3,<hi type="italic">c</hi>).
entries.4a8e2ce2665eba0051ad824f80756227ca7b1063: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.28">Isa 40:28</reference> <div eID="gen13343" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13344" type="x-p"/> The groundlessness of such despondency is set before them in a double question. <hi type="italic">“Is it not known to thee, or hast thou not heard, an eternal God is Jehovah, Creator of the ends of the earth: He fainteth not, neither becomes weary; His understanding is unsearchable.”</hi> Those who are so desponding ought to know, if not from their own experience, at least from information that had been handed down, that Jehovah, who created the earth from one end to the other, so that even Babylonian was not beyond the range of His vision or the domain of His power, was an eternal God, i.e., a God eternally the same and never varying, who still possessed and manifested the power which He had displayed in the creation. Israel had already passed through a long history, and Jehovah had presided over this, and ruled within it; and He had not so lost His power in consequence, as to have now left His people to themselves. He does not grow faint, as a man would do, who neglected to take the repeated nourishment requisite to sustain the energy of his vital power; nor does He become weary, like a man who has exhausted his capacity for work by over-exertion. And if He had not redeemed His people till then, His people were to know that His course was pure <hi type="italic">tebhūnâh</hi> or understanding, which was in the possession of infallible criteria for determining the right point of time at which to interpose with His aid.
entries.8322fa109d86b31b6cf6cb4a735ec11c1df89098: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.29">Isa 40:29</reference> <div eID="gen13344" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13345" type="x-p"/> Jehovah is so far from becoming faint, that it is He who gives strength to the fainting. <hi type="italic">“Giving power to the faint, and to the incapable He giveth strength in abundance.”</hi> אונים לאין is equivalent to אונים איןלאשׁר אין is used exactly like a privative to form a negative adjective (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.88.5">Psa 88:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.25.3">Pro 25:3</reference>).
entries.9270a1ebc0acde29e0f8717142eab3c8fee85687: <reference osisRef="Isa.40.30-Isa.40.31">Isa 40:30-31</reference> <div eID="gen13345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13346" type="x-p"/> Faith is all that is needed to ensure a participation in the strength (עצמה after the form חכמה), which He so richly bestows and so powerfully enhances. <hi type="italic">“And youths grow faint and weary, and young men suffer a fall. But they who wait for Jehovah gain fresh strength; lift up their wings like eagles; run, and are not weary; go forward, and do not faint.”</hi> Even youths, even young men in the early bloom of their morning of life (<hi type="italic">bachūrı̄m</hi>, youths, from בּחר, related to בּכר, בּגר), succumb to the effects of the loss of sustenance or over-exertion (both futures are defective, the first letter being dropped), and any outward obstacle is sufficient to cause them to fall (נכשׁל with <hi type="italic">inf. abs. kal</hi>, which retains what has been stated for contemplation, according to Ges. §131, 3, Anm. 2). In <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.40.30">Isa 40:30</reference></hi> the verb stands first, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.30">Isa 40:30</reference> being like a concessive clause in relation to Isa 40:31. “Even though this may happen, it is different with those who wait for Jehovah,” i.e., those who believe in Him; for the Old Testament applies to faith a number of synonyms denoting trust, hope, and longing, and thus describes it according to its inmost nature, as <hi type="italic">fiducia</hi> and as hope, directed to the manifestation and completion of that which is hoped for. The <hi type="italic">Vav cop.</hi> introduces the antithesis, as in Isa 40:8. החליף, to cause one to pursue, or new to take the place of the old (Lat. <hi type="italic">recentare</hi>). The expression וגו יעלוּ is supposed by early translators, after the Sept., Targ. Jer., and Saad., to refer to the moulting of the eagle and the growth of the new feathers, which we meet with in <reference osisRef="Ps.103.5">Psa 103:5</reference> (cf., Mic 1:16) as a figurative representation of the renewal of youth through grace. But Hitzig correctly observes that העלה is never met with as the causative of the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> used in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.6">Isa 5:6</reference>, and moreover that it would require נוצה instead of אבר. The proper rendering therefore is, “they cause their wings to rise, or lift their wings high, like the eagles” (<hi type="italic">'ēbher</hi> as in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.7">Psa 55:7</reference>). Their course of life, which has Jehovah for its object, is as it were possessed of wings. They draw from Him strength upon strength (see <reference osisRef="Ps.84.8">Psa 84:8</reference>); running does not tire them, nor do they become faint from going ever further and further. <div eID="gen13346" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13347" type="x-p"/> The first address, consisting of three parts (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.1-Isa.40.11">Isa 40:1-11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.12-Isa.40.26">Isa 40:12-26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.27-Isa.40.31">Isa 40:27-31</reference>), is here brought to a close. Second Prophecy - Isaiah 41 <div eID="gen13347" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The God of the World’s History and of Prophecy</title> <div sID="gen13348" type="x-p"/> Jehovah comes forward here, and speaking in the tone in which He already began to speak in <reference osisRef="Isa.40.25">Isa 40:25</reference>, invites the idolatrous nations to contend with Him, declares the raising up of the conqueror from the east to be His work, and adduces this as the sign that He has been the Author and Guider of the world’s history from the beginning. But what if the question should be asked on the part of the nations, With what right does He do this? The acts of the conqueror prove themselves to be a work of the God who is exalted above the idols, from the fact that they bring destruction to the idolatrous nations, and to the people of Jehovah the long-desired redemption. It is in this that the conclusiveness of the illustration lies. The argument, however, presupposes that Cyrus has already entered upon his victorious course. It is evident at the outset that future events, or events still unfulfilled, would have no force as present proofs. And the words also clearly imply, that the work which Jehovah attributes to Himself, in opposition to the gods of the nations, is already in progress.  <chapter eID="Isa.40"/> <div eID="gen13348" type="x-p"/>

entries.270ab643fe24311641387eaf9b8f0a6e6c63063e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.1" sID="gen47877" type="section"/> <div sID="gen47878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi><hi type="italic"> Comfort ye. </hi>The Prophet introduces a new subject; for, leaving the people on whom no favorable impression was made either by threatenings or by admonitions, on account of their desperate wickedness, he turns to posterity, in order to declare that the people who shall be humbled under the cross will experience no want of consolation even amidst the severest distresses. And it is probable that he wrote this prophecy when the time of the captivity was at hand, that he might not at his departure from life leave the Church of God overwhehned by very grievous calamities, without the hope of restoration. Though he formerly mingled his predictions with threatenings and terrors for this purpose, yet he appears to have contemplated chiefly the benefit of those who lived at that time. What will afterwards follow will relate to the future Church, the revival of which was effected long after his death; for he will next lay down a perpetual doctrine, which must not be limited to a single period, and especially when he treats of the commencement and progress of the reign of Christ. And this prophecy must be of so much the greater importance to us, because it addresses us in direct terms; for, although it may be a spiritual application of what goes before, so as to be doctrine that is common both to the Jews and to us, yet, as he leaves the Jews of that age, and addresses posterity down to the end of the world, it appears to belong more especially to us.<div eID="gen47878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47879" type="x-p"/>By this exhortation, therefore, the Lord intended to stir up the hearts of the godly, that they might not faint, amidst heavy calamities. First, he addresses the Jews, who were soon after to be carried into that hard captivity in which they should have neither sacrifices nor prophets, and would have been destitute of all consolation, had not the Lord relieved their miseries by these predictions. Next, he addresses all the godly that should live afterwards, or that shall yet live, to encourage their heart, even when they shall appear to be reduced very low and to be utterly ruined.<div eID="gen47879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47880" type="x-p"/>That this discourse might have greater weight, and might mere powerfully affect their minds, he represents God as raising up new prophets, whom he enjoins to soothe the sorrows of the people by friendly consolation. The general meaning is, that, when he shall have appeared to have forsaken for a time the wretched captives, the testimony of his grace will again burst forth from the darkness, and that, when gladdening prophecies shall have ceased, their proper time will come round. In order to exhibit more strongly the ground of joy, he makes use of the plural number, <hi type="italic">Comfort ye; </hi>by which he intimates that he will send not one or another, but a vast multitude of prophets; and this he actually accomplished, by which we see more clearly his infinite goodness and mercy.<div eID="gen47880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47881" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Will say. </hi>First, it ought to be observed that the verb is in the future tense; and those commentators who render it in the present or past tense both change the words and spoil the meaning. Indircetly he points out an intermediate period, during which the people would be heavily afflicted, as if God had been silent. <note n="104"> <div sID="gen47882" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Comme si Dieu n’en cust rien veu</foreign>.” “As if God had not at all seen it.”<div eID="gen47882" type="x-p"/> </note> Though even at that time God did not cease to hold out the hope of salvation by some prophets, yet, having for a long period cast them off, when they were wretchedly distressed and almost ruined, the consolation was less abundant, till it was pointed out, as it were with the finger, that they were at liberty to return. On this account the word <hi type="italic">comfort </hi>must be viewed as relating to a present favor; and the repetition of the word not only confirms the certainty of the prediction, but applauds its power and success, as if he had said, that in this message there will be abundant, full, and unceasing cause of joy.<div eID="gen47881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47883" type="x-p"/>Above all, we must hold by the future tense of this verb, because there is an implied contrast between that melancholy silence of which I have spoken, and the doctrine of consolation which afterwards followed. And with this prediction agrees the complaint of the Church,<div eID="gen47883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47884" type="x-p"/>“We do not see our signs; there is no longer among us a prophet or any one that knows how long.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.74.9">Psalm 74:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen47884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47885" type="x-p"/>We see how she laments that she has been deprived of the best kind of comfort, because no promise is brought forward for soothing her distresses. It is as if the Prophet bad said, “The Lord will not suffer you to be deprived of prophets, to comfort you amidst your severest distresses. At that time he will raise up men by whom he will send to you the message that had been long desired, and at that time also he will show that he takes care of you.”<div eID="gen47885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47886" type="x-p"/>I consider the future tense, <hi type="italic">will say, </hi>as relating not only to the captivity in Babylon, but to the whole period of deliverance, which includes the reign of Christ. <note n="105"> <div sID="gen47887" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui comprend en soy le regne de Christ jusqu’ a la fin du monde</foreign>.” “Which includes the reign of Christ till the end of the world.”<div eID="gen47887" type="x-p"/> </note> To the verb <hi type="italic">will say, </hi>we must supply “to the prophets,” whom he will appoint for that purpose; for in vain would they have spoken, if the Lord had not told them, and even put into their mouth what they should make known to others. Thus there is a mutual relation between God and the prophets,” whom he will appoint for that purpose; for in vain would they have spoken, if the Lord had not told them and even put into their mouth what they should make known to others. Thus there is a mutual relation between God and the prophets. In a word, the Lord promises that the hope of salvation will be left, although the ingratitude of men deserves that this voice shall be perpetually silenced and altogether extinguished.<div eID="gen47886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47888" type="x-p"/>These words, I have said, ought not to be limited to the captivity in Babylon; for they have a very extensive meaning, and include the doctrine of the gospel, in which chiefly lies the power of “comforting.” To the gospel it belongs to comfort those who are distressed and cast down, to quicken those who are slain and actually dead, to cheer the mourners, and, in short, to bring all joy and gladness; and this is also the reason why it is called “the Gospel,” that is, good news, <note n="106"> <div sID="gen47889" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="fr">Evangile, c’est a dire Bonne nouvelle</foreign>.<div eID="gen47889" type="x-p"/> </note> Nor did it begin at the time when Christ appeared in the world, but long before, since the time when God’s favor was clearly revealed, and Daniel might be said to have first raised his banner, that believers might hold themselves in readiness for returning. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Dan.9.2">Daniel 9:2</reference>.) Afterwards, Haggai, Zechariah, Malachi, Nehemiah, Ezra, and others, down to the coming of Christ, exhorted believers to cherish better and better hopes. Malachi, the last of them that wrote, knowing that there would be few prophets, sends the people to the law of Moses, to learn from it the will of God and its threatenings and promises.
