Besides, this metaphor shews how ridiculous is the blindness of men when they claim anything for themselves; for they gain by their boastings just as much as if some small creatures, such as locusts, would elevate themselves by leaping; but they must immediately fall back on the earth.<div eID="gen47997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47998" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Spreadeth it out as a tent. </hi>David also employs the same form of expression, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.104.2">Psalm 104:2</reference>,) and both speak of the aspect and spreading out of the heavens with respect to us; for they do not mean that God spreads out the heavens, that he may dwell in them, but rather that there may be given to us a place of habitation under them; for while the earth sustains, the heavens cover us, so that we have a dwelling close and covered on all sides.<div eID="gen47998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen47999" type="x-p"/>But it may be thought that these metaphors detract greatly from the dignity of the subject of which the Prophet discourses, while his object is to commend and exalt it to the utmost of his power. What is a <hi type="italic">curtain? </hi>What is a <hi type="italic">tent? </hi>I reply, these metaphors tend nevertheless to exalt the <hi type="italic">subject; </hi>for it is as if he had said, “that it is as easy for God to spread out heaven, as for a man to spread out a curtain.” And he leaves to every person to consider how great is the difference between heaven and a curtain, and what is their size, which any person may easily understand. Lastly, there is an implied contrast between tabernacles or houses <note n="119"> <div sID="gen48000" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="fr">Les maisons</foreign>.<div eID="gen48000" type="x-p"/> </note> which men are long, and laboriously, and at great expense employed in building, and yet which hardly rise to a hundred feet, and the immeasurable height of the heavens spread out by an instantaneous act of the will of God, which makes abundantly manifest how great and how excellent a workman he is.<div eID="gen47999" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen47995" osisID="Isa.40.22" type="section"/>
entries.f066bb1389c2176217bd3c5b4d77dfc48571c3b8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.23" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.23" sID="gen48001" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48002" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23. </hi><hi type="italic">He bringeth the mighty to nothing. </hi>He proceeds in extolling the providence of God, by which he governs the whole world, but more especially mankind. Already and but a little ago he had begun to remark that God did not create the world, so as afterwards to allow it to be governed by chance, but that he undertakes the preservation of it, and keeps it under his power and authority; but as he deigns to look more closely at mankind, so the Prophet selects this department, that by means of it he may extol God’s providence. The sum of what he says is, that God’s government extends far and wide, so that he directs and governs everything according to his pleasure; but he shews, (what was also highly advantageous to be known,) that even in the life of men striking proofs of the immediate exercise of the power of God are visible, and, not even satisfied with the general doctrine, he brings forward one class which ought still more to arouse our attention.<div eID="gen48002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48003" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">The governors of the earth as if they were not.</hi> <note n="120"> <div sID="gen48004" type="x-p"/> “He maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.” — Eng. Ver. “The judges (or rulers) of the earth like emptiness (or desolation) he has made.” —<hi type="italic"> Alexander.</hi><div eID="gen48004" type="x-p"/> </note> Anything that happens to the undistinguished mass of common people is despised and passed by as unworthy of being observed; but when kingdoms and monarchies, or men of high rank, fall from their elevation, it seems as if the earth had been shaken; and the Prophet skilfully avails himself of such proofs to arouse us. It might, indeed, be supposed that princes and magistrates are exempted from the common lot, and are not subject to the ordinary miseries of men; for by their splendor they dazzle the eyes and understandings of all men. But their lustre is entirely dimmed; and therefore the Prophet especially mentions them, and declares that the Lord “bringeth them to nothing.” And if the hand of God is so powerful against nobles and princes, what must we think of the common people? Will he not also treat the ordinary crowd according to his pleasure, and drive them wherever he thinks fit? Will he not either give or take away from them, whenever he pleases, both strength and courage?<div eID="gen48003" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.23" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48001" osisID="Isa.40.23" type="section"/>
entries.9b9029097ad7759b91306dc29e567ef37e4f2b3f: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.24" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.24" sID="gen48005" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> <hi type="italic">It is as if they had not been planted. </hi>Though the particle <foreign xml:lang="he">אף</foreign> (<hi type="italic">aph</hi>) signifies <hi type="italic">also, </hi>yet in this passage it may be more appropriately rendered “so that;” and thus the plain meaning will be, “So that you may say that they were not planted or sown.” It is an amplification of what he had formerly said, for he shews that the princes are totally destroyed and rooted out, so that no trace of them is left, any more than if they had never existed. So long as they remain in prosperity, they appear to be so strong as to be beyond the possibility of being thrown down by any adverse event. <note n="121"> <div sID="gen48007" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Que le vent d’adversite ne les puisse abattre</foreign>.” “That the wind of adversity cannot throw them down.”<div eID="gen48007" type="x-p"/> </note> but such changes happen as blot out their name and remembrance, so that you would say that they had never existed; and we see that this has happened not only to men but even to very flourishing kingdoms.<div eID="gen48006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48008" type="x-p"/>Since, therefore, great downfalls are so many tokens of God’s dreadful power, let us learn not to lean on earthly and deceitful supports, but, whatever may be the amount of our riches or strength, let us depend on him. God does not, as heathen men babble, turn about this world like a ball, as if he took pleasure in this game; but whenever any person is highly elevated, he never ceases from insolent boasting till he is thrown down headlong, so that the judgments of God are always manifest. We are also reminded by it, that it is wrong to ascribe to fortune or to any other cause the various events that happen; for God was not an instantaneous Creator, that would immediately abandon the charge of his work, but incessantly applies his hand, so that nothing is done but by his will and pleasure. Seeing that various changes thus happen in the world, seeing that those things which were thought to be firm and stable are transitory and fading, let us turn our minds to that supreme providence of God.<div eID="gen48008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48009" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Even while he bloweth on them. </hi>Hence he shows how light and trivial before God are those things which commonly dazzle our eyes and fill us with amazement; for we cannot think of any great king without being perfectly alarmed and stupified. But he shows that kings and princes are like stubble before God, by whose breath they are driven, as by a whirlwind, at any instant that he pleases. We are therefore taught that we ought never to be overwhelmed by the sight of any creature, so as not to render to God the honor and glory that are due to him. This ought to have been carefully considered by the Jews, who would have thought that that monarchy of the Babylonians, whose captives they were, would never be destroyed, and that they could not be rescued out of their hands, if they had not called to remembrance this doctrine, that nothing in this world is so durable that it may not be dissolved by the breath of God. That they may not despair of their salvation, the Prophet reminds them that God, as soon as he shall be pleased to thunder from heaven, will crush all that strength in their enemies that terrifies them, so that it shall vanish away.<div eID="gen48009" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.24" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48005" osisID="Isa.40.24" type="section"/>
entries.07ef7b70e55eb5fe8801940e03f134f2e63941f4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.25" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.25" sID="gen48010" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48011" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> <hi type="italic">And to whom will ye liken me? </hi>He repeats the former statement, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.40.18">verse 18</reference>,) by which he said that the Lord would not suffer himself to be likened to idols; that the Jews might not in any degree detract, from his power, on account of their having been so long held captive in the hand of unbelievers, or think that idols are anything on account of the prosperity of their worshippers, whom they were compelled to serve; for, by reasoning in this manner about the power of the true God and of idols, they would have compared him with idols. On this account he repeats, as it were in indignation, “To whom will ye liken me?” as if he had said, “Will you rob me of my majesty by your comparisons?” For although men have various thoughts of God, and transform him according to their fancy, yet he continues to be like himself, for he does not change his nature on account of the inventions of men.<div eID="gen48011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48012" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Saith the Holy One. </hi>He appropriately applies to God the term <hi type="italic">Holy, </hi>by which title he indirectly blames or accuses the Jews of base ingratitude, if, as they have been set apart by him, they do not sanctify him in return. No holiness will be found in the gods of the Gentiles; they are the mere inventions of men. A grievous injury therefore is done to God, and he is basely degraded from his rank, when idols are brought into collision with him, and when it becomes a subject of debate if they can do more than God himself.<div eID="gen48012" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.25" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48010" osisID="Isa.40.25" type="section"/>
entries.4e7e477c0a1546e4e58bef2cc57627e41a491a55: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.26" sID="gen48013" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48014" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> <hi type="italic">Lift up your eyes on high. </hi>The Prophet appears to linger too long on this subject, more especially because it presents no obscurity; for he repeats by many statements what is acknowledged by all, that God’s wonderful power and wisdom may be known from the beautiful order of the world. But we ought to observe what I have already said, that we are so wicked and ungrateful judges of the divine power, that we often imagine God to be inferior to some feeble man. We are more terrified frequently by the empty mask of a single man <note n="122"> <div sID="gen48015" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">L’apparence d’un ver de terre</foreign>.” “The appearance of a worm of the earth.”<div eID="gen48015" type="x-p"/> </note> than we are strengthened by all the promises of God. Not in vain, therefore, does the Prophet repeat that God is defrauded of his honor, if his power do not lead us to warm admiration of him; nor does he spend his labor in what is superfluous, for we are so dull and sluggish that we need to be continually aroused and excited.<div eID="gen48014" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48016" type="x-p"/>Men see every day the heavens and the stars; but who is there that thinks about their Author? By nature men are formed in such a manner as to make it evident that they were born to contemplate the heavens, and thus to learn their Author; for while God formed other animals to look downwards for pasture, he made man alone erect, and bade him look at what may be regarded as his own habitation.<div eID="gen48016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48017" type="x-p"/>This is also described beautifully by a poet: <note n="123"> <div sID="gen48018" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Par un poete profane</foreign>.” “By a heathen poet.”<div eID="gen48018" type="x-p"/> </note> “While other animals look downwards towards the earth, he gave to man a lofty face, and bade him look at heaven, and lift up his countenance erect towards the stars.” <note n="124"> <div sID="gen48019" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48020" type="x-p"/>“<foreign xml:lang="la">Pronaque quum spectent animalia caetera terram, <lb/> Os homini sublime dedit, coelumque videre <lb/> Jussit, et erectos ad sidera tollere vultus</foreign>.”<div eID="gen48020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48021" type="x-p"/>Some readers will, perhaps, thank me for a translation of the above passage into French rhyme, taken from the French version of this Commentary. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen48021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48022" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">“</hi><foreign xml:lang="fr"><hi type="italic">Et</hi> <hi type="italic">neantmoins que tout autre animal <lb/> Iette toujours son regard principal <lb/> En contre bas, Dieu a Phomme a donne <lb/> La face haute, et luy a ordonne <lb/> De regarder l’excellence des cieux, <lb/> Et d’eslever aux estoilles ses yeux</hi></foreign><hi type="italic">.”</hi><div eID="gen48022" type="x-p"/> </note> The Prophet therefore points out the wickedness of men who do not acknowledge what is openly placed before their eyes concerning God, but, like cattle, fix their snout in the earth; for, whenever we raise our eyes upwards, with any degree of attention, it is impossible for our senses not to be struck with the majesty of God.<div eID="gen48017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48023" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And see who hath created them. </hi>By mentioning the stars, he states more clearly that the wonderful order which shines brightly in the face of the heavens preaches loudly that there is one God and Creator of the world; and all who shall observe, that amidst the vast number and variety of the stars, so regular an order and course is so well maintained, will be constrained to make this acknowledgment. For it is not by chance that each of the stars has had its place assigned to it, nor is it at random that they advance uniformly with so great rapidity, and amidst numerous windings move straight forwards, so that they do not deviate a hairbreadth from the path which God has marked out for them. Thus does their wonderful arrangement shew that God is the Author and worker, so that men cannot open their eyes without being constrained to behold the majesty of God in his works.<div eID="gen48023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48024" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Bringing out by number their army. </hi>Under the word <hi type="italic">army </hi>he, includes two things; their almost infinite number, and their admirable arrangement; for a small number of persons do not constitute an army, and not even a considerable number, if there be not also numerous companies. Besides, it is not called an “army,” when men are collected together at random, and without any selection, and in a confused manner, or when they wander about in a disorderly state, but where there are various classes of officers, who have the charge of ten, or a hundred, or a thousand men, <note n="125"> <div sID="gen48025" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais celle ou il y aura des sergens de bande, capitaines, colonels et autres conducteurs</foreign>.” “But where there shall be serjeants of companies, captains, colonels, and other officers.”<div eID="gen48025" type="x-p"/> </note> and where the ranks are drawn up and arranged on a fixed plan. Thus the wonderful arrangement of the stars, and their certain courses, may justly be called an “army.”<div eID="gen48024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48026" type="x-p"/>By the word <hi type="italic">number </hi>he means that God always has this “army” at his command. In an army the soldiers may wander, and may not be immediately collected or brought back to their ranks by the general, though the trumpet sound. But it is otherwise with God. He always has his soldiers in readiness, and that “by number;” that is, he keeps a reckoning of them, so that not one of them is absent.<div eID="gen48026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48027" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">He will call to all of them by name. </hi>The same expression occurs, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.147.4">Psalm 147:4</reference>,) and in the same sense. Some explain it to mean that God knows the number of the stars, which is unknown to us. But David and Isaiah meant a different thing, that is, that God makes use of the stars according to his pleasure; as if one should command a servant, calling him to him by name; and the same thing will afterwards be said of Cyrus, whose labors and service the Lord employed in delivering his people. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.45.1">Isaiah 45:1</reference>.) In a word, it denotes the utmost submission and obedience, when he who is called instantly answers to his name.<div eID="gen48027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48028" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">By the greatness of his strength. </hi>Those who explain the preceding clause to mean that the Lord knows the number of the stars, are also mistaken in supposing that by giving them their names is meant their power and office. Others explain it, that there is not a star that has not its own power and energy, because the Lord gave to them those qualities they would always possess. But others connect these words with <foreign xml:lang="he">יקרא</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(yikra,)</hi> “he shall call;” as if he had said, “The Lord is so powerful that all the stars listen to his commands.” But a meaning which appears to me to be more appropriate is, that God is so powerful, that, as soon as he has issued an order, all the armies of the stars are ready to yield obedience. In this we have an extraordinary proof of his power, when those highly excellent, creatures unhesitatingly submit to him, and by executing his orders testify that they acknowledge him to be their Author.<div eID="gen48028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48029" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Not one shall be wanting. </hi>The word <foreign xml:lang="he">איש</foreign> <hi type="italic">(ish) </hi>is applied by Hebrew writers not only to men and women, but also to other animals, and even to inanimate objects, as in a former passage, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.34.16">Isaiah 34:16</reference>,) when, speaking of the birds that should occupy those splendid abodes, he said that “<hi type="italic">not</hi> <hi type="italic">one </hi>should be wanting,” he used the word <foreign xml:lang="he">איש</foreign><hi type="italic">(ish).</hi> <note n="126"> <div sID="gen48030" type="x-p"/> In the passage referred to, although not <foreign xml:lang="he">איש</foreign> (<hi type="italic">ish</hi>) but the feminine form <foreign xml:lang="he">אשה</foreign> <hi type="italic">(ishshah) </hi>is used, this does not invalidate our author’s argument. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen48030" type="x-p"/> </note> These words commend to us the power of God, that we may know that there is nothing in heaven or in earth that does not depend on his will and pleasure. Nothing, therefore, can be more shameful or unreasonable than to compare him to idols, which are as worthless as anything can possibly be. <note n="127"> <div sID="gen48031" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Qui sont plus vaines que la vanite mesme</foreign>.” “Which are more vain than vanity itself.”<div eID="gen48031" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen48029" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48013" osisID="Isa.40.26" type="section"/>
entries.a6ec367da586d9a074720adc51fbb0a99f67ee6c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.27" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.27" sID="gen48032" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi><hi type="italic"> Why wilt thou say? </hi>The Prophet now expostulates either with the Jews, because they were almost overcome by despair, and did not look to the promises of God, by which they ought, to have supported their minds; or he makes provision for posterity, that they may not sink under any distresses however long continued. The verbs are in the future sense, which might also be explained by the subjunctive mood, <hi type="italic">Why wouldst thou say?</hi> For Isaiah justly infers front the preceding statement, that the chosen people, whatever may happen, ought to wait patiently for God, till he give assistance in due time. He argues from the less to the greater: “Since God keeps every part of the world under his authority, it is impossible that he shall forsake his Church.” Yet it is probable that at that time there were heard among the people complaints, by which they murmured against God, as if he did not care about their salvation, or were slow in rendering assistance, or even shut his eyes and did not see their distresses. The fault which is now corrected is, that they thought that God did not care about them; as usually happens in afflictions, in which we think that God has forsaken us, and exposed us for a prey, and that he takes no concern about the affairs of this world. <note n="128"> <div sID="gen48034" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Et qu’il ne se soucie des choses de ce monde</foreign>.”<div eID="gen48034" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen48033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48035" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">O Jacob and Israel! </hi>By these names he calls to their remembrance the Lord’s covenant, which had been ratified by promises so numerous and so diversified; as if he had said, “Dost thou not think that thou art that people which God hath chosen peculiarly for himself? Why dost thou imagine that he who cannot deceive does not attend to thy cause?”<div eID="gen48035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48036" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">My way is hidden from Jehovah. </hi>He employs the word <hi type="italic">way </hi>for “condition” and ‘cause,” and <hi type="italic">hidden, </hi>for “disregarded” or “unknown;” for if God delay his assistance for a short time, we think that his care does not extend to us. Some explain it differently, that is, that the people are here reproved for thinking that they would not be punished for sinning, and they think that this sentiment resembles such as, “The wicked man hath said in his heart, There is no God.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.14.1">Psalm 14:1</reference>.) But the Prophets meaning unquestionably was, “Thinkest thou, O Israel, that the Lord taketh no concern about thine affairs?” For he exclaims against the distrust of the people, and chides them sharply, that he may afterwards comfort them, and may show that the Lord will continually assist his people whom he hath undertaken to defend.<div eID="gen48036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48037" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And my judgment passeth away from my God. </hi>The word <hi type="italic">judgment </hi>confirms our interpretation of the preceding clause; for “judgment” is implored in affliction, when we are unjustly oppressed, or when any one does us wrong; and God is said to favor and undertake “judgment,” or “our right,” when, after having known our cause, he defends and guards us; and he is said to <hi type="italic">pass by it, </hi>when he overlooks us, and permits us to be devoured by our enemies. It is as if he had said, that the Jews act unjustly in complaining that God has disregarded their cause and forsaken them; and by that reproof he prepares them for receiving consolation, for they could not receive it while their minds were occupied with wicked or foolish thoughts. It was therefore necessary first to remove obstructions, and to open up the way for consolation.<div eID="gen48037" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.27" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48032" osisID="Isa.40.27" type="section"/>
entries.0cd01e38116f9e06acdf49512a854f818bb71f04: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.28" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.28" sID="gen48038" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48039" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> <hi type="italic">Hast thou not known? </hi>He repeats the same statement which he had formerly made, that the people who had been carefully taught in the school of God were inexcusable for their slothfulness, and chides them sharply for not having profited more by the doctrine of the Law, and by the other means which God had bestowed in addition to that knowledge which they possessed in common with the Gentiles. The word <hi type="italic">know, </hi>which is more general, is put first; because by many miracles and other proofs God had manifested his glory. Next, he asks, <hi type="italic">Hast thou not heard?</hi> As if he had said, “If thou hast profited nothing by being taught by actions and by word that God is never unemployed, it is evident that thou are excessively unteachable.”<div eID="gen48039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48040" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">That Jehovah is the God of eternity. </hi>The Prophet calls him “eternal,” and thus distinguishes him from all idols, which endure but for a time, and were made by men; and truly, if this were deeply seated in our hearts, there would no longer be any room for distrust; for if God is eternal, he never changes or decays, eternity being uniformly attended by this quality, that it is never liable to change, but always remains the same. Since the Jews did not sufficiently believe these things, though they had often “heard” them, the Prophet intended to arouse them by this reproof, in order to shew that they will be doubly guilty before God, if, after having been taught both by his numerous benefits, and by the word, they do not render the honor and glory which are due to him.<div eID="gen48040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48041" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And is not wearied by weariness, and there is no searching of his understanding. </hi>Here the Prophet makes two statements; first, that God is not wearied in doing good; and, secondly, that no man can explore his wisdom. In the former clause he shews that, nothing will hinder God from continuing to exercise his kindness; for he is not like men whose resources are exhausted by giving frequently, or who are wearied by continually bestowing new favors, or who repent of their generosity. His kindness is never exhausted; if he was kind to the fathers, he will be not less kind and bountiful to posterity. As to the allegation, that God very often acts differently from what we think to be best for us, the Prophet meets it by saying that his purpose is incomprehensible, and warns us that we ought not to murmur, though he does not all at once comply with our wishes; because nothing is better adapted to cherish our hope than this sobriety, which leads us to consider how marvellously God works in preserving us, and thus to submit to his secret counsel.<div eID="gen48041" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.28" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48038" osisID="Isa.40.28" type="section"/>
entries.20d2cce00be11157e85f0f76d9a9a2a7e976b511: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.29" sID="gen48042" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48043" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> <hi type="italic">He giveth power to the faint. </hi>The Prophet now applies to the present subject the general statements which he made; for we have said that his intention was to give warmer encouragement to the people, and to lead them to cherish better hope. Because the Jews were at that time weakened and destitute of all strength, he shews that on this account it belongs to God to give assistance to those who were thus exhausted and weakened. He therefore magnifies the power of God on this ground, that they may conclude and believe that they ought not to doubt of their salvation so long as they enjoy his favor. It was indeed to the people who were held captive in Babylon that the Prophet looked; but we ought also to apply this doctrine to ourselves, that whenever our strength shall fail, and we shall be almost laid low, we may call to remembrance that the Lord stretches out his hand ‘to the faint,” who are sinking through the want of all help. But first, we must feel our faintness and poverty, that the saying of Paul, “The power of God is made perfect in our weakness,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.12.9">2 Corinthians 12:9</reference>,) may be fulfilled; for if our hearts are not deeply moved by a conviction of our weakness, we cannot receive seasonable assistance from God.<div eID="gen48043" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48042" osisID="Isa.40.29" type="section"/>
entries.210185d443a8e6be46c2f64dc3ccf9ab7d56ede1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.30" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.30" sID="gen48044" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48045" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">30.</hi> <hi type="italic">The youths are wearied and faint. </hi>By this comparison the Prophet illustrates more powerfully what he had formerly said, that the strength which God imparts to his elect is invincible and unwearied; for men’s strength easily fails, but God’s strength never fails. It is indeed certain that all the vigor which naturally dwells in us proceeds from God; but since men claim as their own what God has bestowed generally on all, the Prophet thus distinguishes between the strength of men which appears to be born with them, and that strength by which God peculiarly supports his elect; for God’s kindness, which is diffused throughout all nature, is not sufficiently perceived. And thus by “men’s strength” he means that which is generally possessed by mankind, and by “God’s assistance,”<hi type="italic"> </hi>he means that by which he peculiarly assists us after our strength has failed; for the Prophet speaks of the grace of God which is cormmonly called supernatural, and says that it is perpetual, while men can have nothing in themselves but what is fading and transitory; that by this mark he may distinguish between the Church of God and the rest of the world, and between spiritual grace and earthly prosperity.<div eID="gen48045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48046" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And the young men by falling fall. </hi>In the former clause he made use of the word <foreign xml:lang="he">נערים</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(negnarim,) youths, </hi>but now he adds <foreign xml:lang="he">בחרים</foreign>, <hi type="italic">(bachurim,) </hi>which means not only that they were “young men,” but also that they had been selected. <note n="129"> <div sID="gen48047" type="x-p"/> “Men in full vigor, <hi type="italic">picked men, </hi>in military <hi type="italic">language.” </hi>—<hi type="italic"> Stock. </hi><div eID="gen48047" type="x-p"/> </note> The repetition of the same statement may be supposed to refer particularly to age, though he means that they were persons of the choicest vigor and in the prime of life. With this design he recommends that excellent privilege which God bestows on his children in preference to other men; that they may be satisfied with their lot, and may bear no envy to earthly men, <note n="130"> <div sID="gen48048" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Aux enfans de ce monde</foreign>.” “To the children of this world.”<div eID="gen48048" type="x-p"/> </note> for that strength of which they boast. In a word, he shews that men are greatly deceived if they are puffed up by confidence in their own strength, for they immediately sink and faint.<div eID="gen48046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48049" type="x-p"/>He appears to allude to what happens every day, that the stronger any person is, the more boldly does he attempt what is exceedingly difficult, and the consequence is, that they who are naturally more robust seldom live to be old men. They think nothing too hard or difficult, they attempt everything, and rashly encounter all dangers; but they give way in the middle of their course, and suffer the punishment of their rashness. The same thing befalls those who are proud of any gift which God has bestowed on them, and are full of confidence in themselves; for all that they have received from God is reduced to nothing, or rather turns to their ruin and destruction; and thus they are justly punished for their insolence.<div eID="gen48049" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.30" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48044" osisID="Isa.40.30" type="section"/>
entries.1a5a436a724d71f0a950792c8082f664219307e8: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.31" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.40.31" sID="gen48050" type="section"/> <div sID="gen48051" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">31.</hi> <hi type="italic">But they that wait for Jehovah. </hi>Hebrew writers employ the phrase, “exchanging strength,” <note n="131"> <div sID="gen48052" type="x-p"/> “The phrase translated ‘they shall gain new strength,’ properly means ‘they shall exchange strength;’ but the usage of the verb determines its specific meaning to be that of changing for the better, or improving. The sense is therefore correctly given in the English Version (‘they shall renew their strength’).” —<hi type="italic"> Alexander.</hi><div eID="gen48052" type="x-p"/> </note> to denote “gathering new strength,” and thus “being restored.” The Prophet therefore shews, that godly persons, who shall hope in God, will not be deficient in strength; and he confirms what he formerly said,<div eID="gen48051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48053" type="x-p"/>“In rest and silence shall be your strength.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.30.15">Isaiah 30:15</reference>.)<div eID="gen48053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48054" type="x-p"/>We must not become agitated, or throw ourselves forward rashly, but “wait” patiently. In this passage, therefore, <hi type="italic">waiting </hi>means nothing else than patience. Violent men dash themselves to pieces by their own eagerness, but the vigor of godly men, though it has less display, and often appears to lie buried while they calmly “wait for” God’s assistance, is refreshed and renewed. We must therefore return to the saying of Paul, that<div eID="gen48054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48055" type="x-p"/>“the power of God is made perfect in our weakness.” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.12.9">2 Corinthians 12:9</reference>.)<div eID="gen48055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48056" type="x-p"/>We must, therefore be fully convinced of our weakness, that we may yield to the power of God. The Jews, who were oppressed by that cruel captivity, had great need of this doctrine; but for us also, during this wretchedly ruinous condition of the Church, it is exceedingly needful.<div eID="gen48056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48057" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They shall raise their wings as eagles. </hi>It is generally believed that the Prophet uses this phrase in the same sense that the Psalmist says,<div eID="gen48057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48058" type="x-p"/>“Thy youth shall be renewed like that of the eagle.” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.103.5">Psalm 103:5</reference>.)<div eID="gen48058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48059" type="x-p"/>It is certain that the “eagle” is very long-lived as compared with other birds.<div eID="gen48059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48060" type="x-p"/>Aristotle and Pliny affirm that it never dies of old age, but of hunger; that is, that when the upper part of the beak becomes too large, it cannot take food into its mouth, and for a long time subsists entirely on what it drinks. One Zaadias, as all Jews are audacious in constructing fables, pretends that the eagle flies upward into the region that is near the sun, and approaches the sun so closely, that its old wings are burned, and other new ones grow in their place; but this is utterly absurd and fabulous. The Prophet means that they who trust in the Lord will be vigorous, like eagles, till the most advanced old age. But seeing that eagles fly higher than other birds, by which they shew remarkable swiftness, which has also given rise to the proverb, “An eagle among the clouds,” this passage may be understood to denote not only long life, but also strength and agility; so that Isaiah, after having shewn that their strength is recruited, adds that they are more vigorous, and ascend to a great height. Such is also the import of what follows, —<div eID="gen48060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48061" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They shall run and shall not be weary. </hi>It is as if he had said, that the Lord will assist them, so that they shall pursue their course without any molestation. It is a figurative expression, by which he intimates that believers <note n="132"> <div sID="gen48062" type="x-p"/> <foreign xml:lang="fr">Les fideles</foreign>.<div eID="gen48062" type="x-p"/> </note> will always be ready to perform their duty with cheerfulness. But it will be said, “There are so many troubles which we must endure in this life; how then does he say that we shall be exempt from weariness?” I reply, believers are indeed distressed and wearied, but they are at length delivered from their distresses, and feel that they have been restored by the power of God; for it happens to them according to the saying of Paul,<div eID="gen48061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48063" type="x-p"/>“While we are troubled on every side, we are not overwhelmed; we are perplexed, but are not in despair; we suffer persecution, but are not forsaken; we are cast down, but are not destroyed.” <lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.4.8 Bible:2Cor.4.9">2 Corinthians 4:8, 9</reference>.)<div eID="gen48063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48064" type="x-p"/>Let us therefore learn to flee to the Lord, who, after we have encountered many storms, will at length conduct us to the harbor; for he who hath opened up a path, and hath commanded us to advance in that course in which he hath placed us, does not intend to assist us only for a single day, and to forsake us in the middle of our course, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.1.6">Philippians 1:6</reference>,) but will conduct us to the goal.<div eID="gen48064" type="x-p"/><div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.40.31" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen48050" osisID="Isa.40.31" type="section"/><div eID="gen47812"/><div eID="gen47810"/> <div sID="gen48065"/> <div sID="gen48066" type="x-p"/>CHAPTER 41.<div eID="gen48066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen48067"/> <table> <row> <cell> <div sID="gen48068" type="x-p"/><reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.41.1-Isa.41.29">Isaiah 41:1-29</reference><div eID="gen48068" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> Keep silence before me, O islands; and let the people renew <hi type="italic">their </hi>strength: let them come near; then let them speak: let us come near together to judgment.<div eID="gen48069" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> Tacete mihi insulae; et colligant populi vires; accedant, tunc loquentur; pariter ad judicium accedamus.<div eID="gen48070" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> Who raised up the righteous <hi type="italic">man </hi>from the east, called him to his foot, gave the nations before him, and made <hi type="italic">him </hi>rule over kings? he gave <hi type="italic">them </hi>as the dust to his sword, <hi type="italic">and </hi>as driven stubble to his bow.<div eID="gen48071" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> Quis excitavit ab oriente justitiam, vocavit eum ad pedem suum, dedit coram co gentes, et reges subjugavit; dedit quasi pulverem gladio ejus, et quasi stipulam propulsam arcui ejus?<div eID="gen48072" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48073" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> He pursued them, <hi type="italic">and </hi>passed safely; <hi type="italic">even </hi>by the way <hi type="italic">that </hi>he had not gone with his feet.<div eID="gen48073" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">3.</hi> Persequutus est cos; evasit in pace, semita qua non ingressus est pes ejus.<div eID="gen48074" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> Who hath wrought and done <hi type="italic">it</hi>, calling the generations from the beginning? I the LORD, the first, and with the last; I <hi type="italic">am </hi>he.<div eID="gen48075" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">4.</hi> Quis designavit, et fecit, vocans nationes ab initio? Ego Iehova prius, et cum novissimis ego idem.<div eID="gen48076" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> The isles saw <hi type="italic">it, </hi>and feared; the ends of the earth were afraid, drew near, and came.<div eID="gen48077" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> Viderunt insulae et timuerunt; extremi fines terrae expaverunt, accesserunt, et venerunt.<div eID="gen48078" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> They helped every one his neighbour; and <hi type="italic">every one </hi>said to his brother, Be of good courage.<div eID="gen48079" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48080" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">6.</hi> Quisque proximo suo opem tulit, et fratri suo dixit, Sis strenuus.<div eID="gen48080" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> So the carpenter encouraged the goldsmith, <hi type="italic">and </hi>he that smootheth <hi type="italic">with </hi>the hammer him that smote the anvil, saying, It <hi type="italic">is </hi>ready for the sodering: and he fastened it with nails, <hi type="italic">that </hi>it should not be moved.<div eID="gen48081" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">7.</hi> Confortavit faber conflatorem, malleo percutiens tundentem vicissim, et dixit, Bonum hoc ad plumbaturam; firmavitque clavis, ut non moveretur.<div eID="gen48082" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> But thou, Israel, <hi type="italic">art </hi>my servant, Jacob whom I have chosen, the seed of Abraham my friend.<div eID="gen48083" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48084" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> At tu Israel servus meus, Iacob quem elegi, semen Abrahae amici mei.<div eID="gen48084" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48085" type="x-p"/>9.<hi type="italic"> Thou </hi>whom I have taken from the ends of the earth, and called thee from the chief men thereof, and said unto thee, Thou <hi type="italic">art </hi>my servant; I have chosen thee, and not cast thee away.<div eID="gen48085" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> Quoniam apprehendi to ab extremitatibus terrae, ab eminentiis ejus vocavi to, ac dixi tibi, Servus meus es tu, elegi to, et non repudiavi to.<div eID="gen48086" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48087" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> Fear thou not; for I <hi type="italic">am </hi>with thee: be not dismayed; for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy God: I will strengthen thee; yea, I will help thee; yea, I will uphold thee with the right hand of my righteousness.<div eID="gen48087" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> Ne timeas, quoniam ego tecum sum; non terrearis, quoniam ego Deus tuus sum, qui to corroboro, adhuc <hi type="italic">(vel, utique) </hi>opem tibi feram, adhuc to sustentabo dextera justitiae meae.<div eID="gen48088" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> Behold, all they that were incensed against thee shall be ashamed and confounded: they shall be as nothing; and they that strive with thee shall perish.<div eID="gen48089" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">11.</hi> Ecce pudefient et erubescent omnes qui to provocant; erunt quasi in nihilum, et peribunt qui tecum litigant.<div eID="gen48090" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> Thou shalt seek them, and shalt not find them, <hi type="italic">even </hi>them that contended with thee: they that war against thee shall be as nothing, and as a thing of nought.<div eID="gen48091" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> Quaeres cos, nee invenies; qui contendunt tecum erunt quasi nihilum, et qui tecum belligerantur, quasi consumptio.<div eID="gen48092" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> For I the LORD thy God will hold thy right hand, saying unto thee, Fear not; I will help thee.<div eID="gen48093" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> Quoniam ego Iehova Deus tuus, apprehendens dextram tuam, ac dicens tibi, Ne timeas, ego tibi opitulabor.<div eID="gen48094" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48095" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> Fear not, thou worm Jacob, <hi type="italic">and </hi>ye men of Israel; I will help thee, saith the LORD, and thy redeemer, the Holy One of Israel.<div eID="gen48095" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> Ne timeas, vermis Iacob, mortui Israel; ego auxiliabor tibi, dicit Iehova, et redemptor <hi type="italic">(vel, vindex) </hi>tuus, Sanctus Israelis.<div eID="gen48096" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> Behold, I will make thee a new sharp threshing instrument having teeth: thou shalt thresh the mountains, and beat <hi type="italic">them </hi>small, and shalt make the hills as chaff.<div eID="gen48097" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> Ecce posui to in traham; ut tribula nova habens dentes, triturabis montes et comminues, et colles in pulverem rediges.<div eID="gen48098" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> Thou shalt fan them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the whirlwind shall scatter them: and thou shalt rejoice in the LORD, <hi type="italic">and </hi>shalt glory in the Holy One of Israel.<div eID="gen48099" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">16.</hi> Ventilabis eos, et ventus toilet, et turbo sparget eos. Tu vero exultabis in Iehova, in Sancto Israel gloriaberis.<div eID="gen48100" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi><hi type="italic"> When </hi>the poor and needy seek water, and <hi type="italic">there is </hi>none, <hi type="italic">and </hi>their tongue faileth for thirst, I the LORD will hear them, I the God of Israel will not forsake them.<div eID="gen48101" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> Egeni et pauperes quaerent aquas, quae non apparent; lingua eorum siti exarebit. Ego Iehova exaudiam cos; ego Deus Israelis non descram eos.<div eID="gen48102" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48103" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> I will open rivers in high places, and fountains in the midst of the valleys: I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water.<div eID="gen48103" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">18.</hi> Aperiam in editis cacuminibus flumina, et fontes in media planitie; desertum ponam in stagna aquarum, et terram vastam in scaturigines aquarum.<div eID="gen48104" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48105" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the shittah-tree, and the myrtle, and the oil tree; I will set in the desert the fir tree, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the pine, and the box tree together:<div eID="gen48105" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">19.</hi> Dabo in deserto cedrum, spinum, myrtum, et pinum; ponam in solitudine abietem, ulmum, et popu-lure sired.<div eID="gen48106" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48107" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> That they may see, and know, and consider, and understand together, that the hand of the LORD hath done this, and the Holy One of Israel hath created it.<div eID="gen48107" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">20.</hi> Itaque videant, et cognoseant, cogitent, et intelligant simul, quod manus Iehovae fecerit hoc, et Sanctus Israelis creaverit istud.<div eID="gen48108" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> Produce your cause, saith the LORD; bring forth your strong <hi type="italic">reasons, </hi>saith the King of Jacob.<div eID="gen48109" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">21.</hi> Adeste cansae vestrae, dicit Iehova; afferte firmamenta vestra, dicit rex Iacob.<div eID="gen48110" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48111" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> Let them bring <hi type="italic">them </hi>forth, and shew us what shall happen: let them shew the former things, what they <hi type="italic">be, </hi>that we may consider them, and know the latter end of them; or declare us things for to come.<div eID="gen48111" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48112" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">22.</hi> Adducant, et annuntient nobis quae ventura sunt; priora quae fuerunt nuntient, et apponemus cor nostrum; et sciemus novissima eorum; et quae ventura sunt praedicate nobis.<div eID="gen48112" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48113" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> Shew the things that are to come hereafter, that we may know that ye<hi type="italic"> are </hi>gods: yea, do good, or do evil, that we may be dismayed, and behold <hi type="italic">it </hi>together.<div eID="gen48113" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48114" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">23.</hi> Nunciate quae futura sunt in posterum, ut sciamus vos deos esse; quin benefacite, ant malefacite, ut enarremus, et videanus <hi type="italic">(vel, mire-mur</hi>) pariter.<div eID="gen48114" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> Behold, ye<hi type="italic"> are </hi>of nothing, and your work of nought: an abomination <hi type="italic">is he that </hi>chooseth you.<div eID="gen48115" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48116" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">24.</hi> Ecce vos estis ex nihilo, et factura vestra ex nihilo; abominationem elegit in vobis (homo.)<div eID="gen48116" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48117" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> I have raised up <hi type="italic">one</hi> from the north, and he shall come: from the rising of the sun shall he call upon my name: and he shall come upon princes as <hi type="italic">upon </hi>morter, and as the potter treadeth clay.<div eID="gen48117" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48118" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">25.</hi> Excitavi ab aquilone, et venit; ab oriente solis vocabit in nomine meo; et veniet ad principes, quasi ad lutum, et tanquam figulus calcabit lutum.<div eID="gen48118" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48119" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> Who hath declared from the beginning, that we may know? and beforetime, that we may say, <hi type="italic">He is </hi>righteous? yea, <hi type="italic">there is </hi>none that sheweth, yea, <hi type="italic">there is </hi>none that dcclareth, yea, <hi type="italic">there is </hi>none that heareth your words.<div eID="gen48119" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48120" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">26.</hi> Quis nuntiavit ab initio, ut cognoscamus? Jam ante, et dicemus, justus. Utique non est annuntians; utique non audire faciens; utique non audiens verba vestra.<div eID="gen48120" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48121" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> The first <hi type="italic">shall say </hi>to Zion, Behold, behold them: and I will give to Jerusalem one that bringeth good tidings.<div eID="gen48121" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48122" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">27.</hi> Primus Sioni, Ecce, ecce ipsi; et Ierosolymae nuntium dabo.<div eID="gen48122" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48123" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> For I beheld, and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no man; even among them, and <hi type="italic">there was </hi>no counsellor, that, when I asked of them, could answer a word.<div eID="gen48123" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48124" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">28.</hi> Aspexi, nec nullus erat; de istis inquisivi, et nullus erat consiliarius; interrogavi cos, nec responderunt verbum.<div eID="gen48124" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row><row> <cell> <div sID="gen48125" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> Behold, they <hi type="italic">are </hi>all vanity; their works <hi type="italic">are</hi> nothing; their molten images <hi type="italic">are </hi>wind and confusion.<div eID="gen48125" type="x-p"/> </cell><cell> <div sID="gen48126" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">29.</hi> Ecce onmes vanitas, et defectus opera; eorum; ventus et chaos simulachra eorum.<div eID="gen48126" type="x-p"/> </cell> </row> </table> <div sID="gen48127" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen48127" type="x-p"/>

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="40" type="chapter">
                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XL.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The Prophet having <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> foretold the <ns0:hi>Babylonish</ns0:hi> Capti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vity, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 39. 6, 7. doth here arm his People against it by the consideration of their certain deliverance out of it, and their blessed condition after it, as in other things so especi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally in the coming of the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> and the great and glori<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous priviledges conferred upon Gods Church and People in his dayes.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. COmfort ye, comfort ye my people <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Ye Prophets and Ministers of the Lord, which now are: Or hereafter shall be, deliver this comfortable message from me to my People, that they may not sink under their bur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dens.</ns0:note>, saith your God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Speak ye <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to the heart.</ns0:note> comfortably to Jerusalem, and cry unto her <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Proclaim it in my name.</ns0:note>, that her <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> appoin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted time.</ns0:note> warfare <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The time of her servitude, and captivity, and misery.</ns0:note> is accomplished, that her iniquity is pardoned <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I am reconciled to her; I will not impute sin to her, to punish her any longer for it.</ns0:note>: for she hath receiv<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of the LORDS hand <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 16. 18. Lam. 1. 12. Dan. 9. 12.</ns0:note> double for all <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Not twice as much as her sins deserved, for she her self confessed the contrary, <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 9. 1<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>
                        <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>Lament.</ns0:hi> 3. 22. but abundantly enough to answer Gods design in this chastile<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment, which was to humble and reform them, and to warn others by their example. <ns0:hi>Double</ns0:hi> is oft put for abundantly, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 61. 7. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 16. 18. and 17. 18. God here speaks of himself after the manner of men, and compareth himself to a tender-hearted Father, who when he hath corrected his Child for his misdemeanour relenteth and repenteth of his severity, and casteth his Rod away.</ns0:note> her sins.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal. 3. 1. Mat. 3. 3. Mark. 1. 3. Luke 3. 4. John 1. 23.</ns0:note> The voice <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">An abrupt and imperfect speech, such as there are ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ny in the <ns0:hi>Hebrew</ns0:hi> Language. Methinks I hear a voice<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Or, a voice shall be heard.</ns0:note> of him that crieth in the wil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derness <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Which words declare the place either. 1. Where the cry was made: Or, 2. Where the way was to be prepared, as it is expressed in the following clause, which is added to explain this. And such places being com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly path-less, and many wayes incommodious to passen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gers, it was the more necessary to prepare a way there. But both come to one thing, for the cry was to be in that place which was to be prepared. This place seems to be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood immediately of the deliverance of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> out of <ns0:hi>Ba<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bylon,</ns0:hi> and of smoothing their passage from thence to <ns0:hi>Iudea,</ns0:hi> which lay through a great Wilderness; but ultimately and principally concerning their Redem<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>on by the <ns0:hi>Messiah,</ns0:hi> whose coming is ushered in by the Cry <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> the Baptist, who did both cry and prepare the way in the Wilderness, as we read, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 3. 1, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Where this Text is directly expound<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed of him. But withal the terms of <ns0:hi>Wilderness</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Desert,</ns0:hi> seem to be here chiefly used in a metaphorical sence, to ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />press the desolate and forlorn condition of the Jewish Na<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, and especially of the Gentile-world, when Christ came to redeem them<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> for so these words are frequently used in prophetical writings, as hath been noted in divers places.</ns0:note>, Prepare ye the way <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">You to whom this work belongs. He alludes to the custom of Princes who send Pioneers before them to prepare the way through which they intend to pass. The meaning is onely this, That God shall by his Spirit so dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pose mens hearts, and by his providence so order the Em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pires and affairs of the World, as to make way for the ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />complishment of this promise.</ns0:note> of the LORD <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>For the Lord</ns0:hi> as it is ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pounded in the next clause, that the Lord may wal<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> in it: Which though it may be understood of their coming out of <ns0:hi>Babylon,</ns0:hi> when God might in some sort be said to march in the head of them, conducting and preserving them, yet it was much more evidently and eminently fulfilled, when Christ who was and is God blessed for ever, came into the World in a visible manner.</ns0:note>, make straight <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either direct in opposition to crooked, or even and level in opposition to the Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains and Valleys mentioned in the next verse.</ns0:note> in the desert a high way for our God.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">

                  <ns0:p n="5">5. Jam. 1. 10. 1 Pet. 1. 24.</ns0:note> All flesh is grass, and all the goodness thereof <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> as the flower of the field <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The Prophet having foretold glorious and wonderful things, which God had declared and determined to do, and suspecting that men <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">

                  <ns0:p n="8">8. The grass withereth, the flower fadeth, but the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">John 12. 34. 1 Pet. 1. 25.</ns0:note> word of our God shall stand for ever <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Whatsoever God hath said shall infallibly come to pass.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> O thou that tellest good tidings to Zion.</ns0:note> O Zion that bringest good tidings <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">O <ns0:hi>Zion,</ns0:hi> to whom the glad tidings of the coming of Christ into the World, and of the Salvation of Mankind by him were first published by Christ and his Apostles, and by whom they were published to all Nations. See <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 9. 7. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 26. 13, 14.</ns0:note>: O Jerusalem, that bringest good tidings, lift up thy voice with strength; lift <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> up, be not afraid <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Lest thou shouldest be found a false Prophet; for it shall certainly be fulfilled.</ns0:note>: say unto<ns0:note place="margin">‖ Or, <ns0:hi>O thou that tellest good tidings to Ieru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> the Cities of Judah <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">To all my People in the several places of their abode, whether Cityes or Countries. Onely he names <ns0:hi>Ci<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tyes</ns0:hi> to intimate, that they also, though they should be destroy<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, yet should afterward be rebuilt, and inhabited again.</ns0:note>, Behold your God <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Take notice of this wonderful Work, and glorious ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearance of your God, who will be visibly<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> present with you, so that men may point at him and say, <ns0:hi>Behold here he is.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. Behold the Lord GOD will come <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> against the strong.</ns0:note> with strong <ns0:hi>hand</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">With invincible strength conquering all his enemies. The word <ns0:hi>Hand</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Arm,</ns0:hi> may very well be understood out of the following clause.</ns0:note>, and his arms shall rule for him <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">He shall need no succours, for his own power shall be sufficient to govern his People, and to destroy his Adversaries.</ns0:note>; behold, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 62. 11.</ns0:note> his reward <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with him <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">He comes furnished with re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />compences as well of Mercy and Blessings for his friends and followers, as of Justice and Vengeance for his enemies.</ns0:note>, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> recom<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pence for his work.</ns0:note> and his work before him <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He carrieth on his work or design effectually, so as none can hinder him: for that is said in Scripture to <ns0:hi>be before a man</ns0:hi> which is in his Power, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 20. 15. and 24. 51. <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> Or <ns0:hi>Work</ns0:hi> is here put for <ns0:hi>the reward of the Work<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> as it is, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 49. 4. and 65. 7. and elsewhere. And so the same thing is repeated in other words, as is very usual.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11. He shall <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 49. 10. Ezek. 34. 23. John 10. 11.</ns0:note> feed his flock like a shepherd, he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> in his bosome, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> shall gently lead those <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> that give suck.</ns0:note> that are with young <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">He shall perform all the Offices of a tender and faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful Shepherd towards his People, carrying himself with great Wisdome and Condescension, and Compassion to every one of them according to their several Capacities and Infirmities.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12. Who hath measured the waters in the hol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />low of his hand <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Who can measure them? for indicative Verbs in the Hebrew Language are oft taken potentially; who can do this and the following things but God? And this discourse of Gods infinite Power and Wisdom, is here conveniently added to give them the greater assurance, that God was able<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> as he had declared himself willing, to do these great and wonderful things which he had promised; and that nei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther men nor false Gods were able to hinder him in it. God is here compared to a mighty Giant, supposed to be so big that he can take up, and hold all the waters of the Sea and Rivers of the whole World in one hand, and span the Heavens, and then take up and weigh the whole Earth with the other hand.</ns0:note>? and meted out heaven with the span, and comprehended the dust of the earth in <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> a tierce.</ns0:note> a measure, and weighed the Moun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tains in scales, and the hills in a balance!</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 21. 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>. & 36. 22, 23. Rom. 11. 34. 1 Cor. 2. 16.</ns0:note> Who hath <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>weighed</ns0:hi> Prov. 16. 1.</ns0:note> directed the spirit of the Lord or <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> man of his counsel.</ns0:note> his counsellour hath taught him <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Who did God either need or take to advise him in any of his Work, either of Creation or the Government of the World? Were they not all the effects of his own sole infinite Wisdom? Therefore though all the Nations of the World contrive and conspire against him, and against this Work of his, as indeed they will do, yet his own coun<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sel shall confound all their devices, and carry on his Work in spight of them.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14. With whom took he counsel, and <ns0:hi>who</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> made him understand.</ns0:note> instructed him, and taught him in the path of judgment <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">How to walk and manage all his Affairs with good Judgment and Discretion.</ns0:note>, and taught him knowledg, and shew<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to him the way of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standings.</ns0:note> understanding?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15. Behold, the nations <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">All the Nations of the World;</ns0:note>, are as a drop of a bucket <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Compared with all the Water in the Bucket wherein are innumerable drops<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> such are they if compared with God.</ns0:note>, and are counted <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">By him, and in comparison of him.</ns0:note>, as the small dust of the balance <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which accidently cleaves to the Bal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lance, but make no alteration in the weight.</ns0:note>; behold, he taketh up the Isles <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Those nu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />merous and vast Countries to which they went from <ns0:hi>Iu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />daea</ns0:hi> by Sea, which are commonly called <ns0:hi>Isles,</ns0:hi> as hath been oft observed.</ns0:note> as a very little thing.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:600" />16. And Lebanon <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not sufficient to burn, nor the beasts thereof sufficient for a burnt-offe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">And although he is pleased to accept of poor and small Sacrifices from his People, yet if men were to offer a Sacri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fice agreeable to his infinite excellency, the whole Forest of <ns0:hi>Lebanon</ns0:hi> could not afford either a sufficient number of Beasts to be sacrificed: Or, a sufficient quantity of Wood to consume the Sacrifice.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17. All nations before him <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either in his eyes: Or, being set against him, as this Hebrew word properly and most usually signifies.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> as <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Dan. 4. 35.</ns0:note> nothing, and they are counted to him <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Either in his Judgment: Or, in comparison of him.</ns0:note> less than nothing <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Less than a thing of nought or of no account or worth: Or, as others render it, <ns0:hi>For nothing.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and vanity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18. To whom then will ye <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 46. 5. Act. 17. 29.</ns0:note> liken God <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This is a proper inference from the foregoing discourse of Gods immense and infinite greatness; from whence he taketh occasion to shew both the folly of those that make mean and visible representations of God, as not the <ns0:hi>Gen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiles</ns0:hi> onely but even some of the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> did; and the utter ina<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bility of Men or Idols to give any opposition to God in the doing of these great Works. And this discourse of the madness of Idolaters prosecuted both here, and in the fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lowing Chapter was designed by God, as a necessary an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tidote whereby the <ns0:hi>Iews</ns0:hi> might be preserved from the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tagion of Idolatry, to which God saw they now had strong inclinations, and would have many and great temptations when they were in Captivity.</ns0:note>? or what likeness will ye compare unto him.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19. The workman melteth a graven image <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He melteth some base Metal into a mould, which giveth it the form of an Image, which afterwards is graven or carved to make it more exact and amiable. Thus the Image oweth all its excellency to the Earth for the matter of it, and to the art of man for the form or fashion of it.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 41. 7. & 44. 12. Jer. 10. 3.</ns0:note> the goldsmith spreadeth it over with gold <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Beaten out into Leaves or Plates.</ns0:note>, and casteth silver chains <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either for Orna<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments: Or, rather for use, to fasten it to a Wall or Pil<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lar, least it should fall down, and be broken in peices. Which is spoken in way of scorn and derisson of such ridi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />culous deities as needed such supports.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20. He that <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> is poor of oblation.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> so impoverished that he hath no oblation <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">That he can hardly procure Mony sufficient to buy the meanest Sacrifice for his God.</ns0:note>, chooseth a tree <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> will not rot; he seeketh unto him a cunning workman <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">He is so mad upon his Idols, that he will one way or other find mony to pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cure the choicest materials, and the help of the best Artist to make his Idol.</ns0:note> to pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pare a graven image <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 41. 7.</ns0:note> shall not be re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moved <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Which after all this cost and art, can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not stir one step out of its place to give you any help.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21. Have ye not known <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To wit, God to be the onely true God, the Maker and Governour of the World, and all its Inhabitants: how can you be ignorant of so evident a truth? He adresseth his speech to the Idolatrous <ns0:hi>Gentiles.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>? have ye not heard? hath it not been told you from the beginning <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">To wit, of the World, as the next clause explains it: Were not these infinite perfections of God manifestly discovered to all man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kind by the Creation of the World?</ns0:note>? have ye not understood from the foundations of the earth?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22. <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>him that sitteth<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                        </ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> he that sitteth <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">As a Judge or Governour upon his Throne:</ns0:note> upon the circle of the earth <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>above the Circle,</ns0:hi> &c. far above this round Earth, ever in the highest Heavens; from whence he looketh down upon the Earth, where men appear to him like Grashoppers. As here we have <ns0:hi>the Cir<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cle of the Earth,</ns0:hi> so elsewhere we read of <ns0:hi>the Circle of Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, Ioh</ns0:hi> 22. 14. and of <ns0:hi>the Circle of the Deep,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Sea, Prov.</ns0:hi> 8. 27. because the form of the Heaven, and Earth, and Sea is circular or round, as is evident both from Sense, and from the Principles of Philosophy.</ns0:note>, and the inhabitants thereof <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> as grashoppers <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Small and Contemptible in his sight. Compare <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 13. 33.</ns0:note>, that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 9. 8. Psal. 104. 2. Chap, 44. 24. Jer. 10. 12.</ns0:note> stretcheth out the heavens as a curtain, and spreadeth them out as a tent to dwell in <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">For the benefit of the Earth and of Mankind, that all parts might partake of its comfortable influences. See on <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 9. 8. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 104. 2.</ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23. That bringeth the <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 12. 21. Psal. 107. 40.</ns0:note> princes to nothing <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">That can at his pleasure destroy all the great Poten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tates of the World.</ns0:note>, he maketh the judges of the earth as vanity.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24. Yea, they <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The Princes and Judges last mentioned.</ns0:note> shall not be planted, yea, they shall not be sown <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">They shall take no root, as it follows, for <ns0:hi>Planting</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Sowing</ns0:hi> are in order to taking root, and are necessary to it.
